item.title: Inside the Collapse of Timberon’s Water District — and the Cleanest Way Out
item.description:
A review of court records, regulatory filings, board minutes, and reporting from Otero County shows a small mountain water utility that has now failed the same way twice — and a state regulator once again weighing whether to take it away from its elected board.

TIMBERON, N.M. — Twice in less than twenty years, New Mexico regulators have looked at the Timberon Water and Sanitation District and asked the same question: should a court simply take it over? The first time, around 2008, it happened — TWSD’s own records show a court-ordered receivership and court-set interim rates.

The second time may be upcoming!

In November 2025, Public Regulation Commission member Patrick O’Connell told fellow commissioners the district “is not functioning” and raised receivership again, asking how many more failures the state needed to see before concluding a fine wasn’t enough.

Between those two moments sits nearly two decades of litigation, tax disputes, open-meetings violations, and — in the past several weeks alone — three boil-water advisories, a hidden drinking-water violation, a golf course leased to a private operator for a dollar a month, a closed swimming pool, and a board move toward foreclosing on more than 200 delinquent ratepayers while the system that serves them keeps failing. Understanding how Timberon got here — and what would actually fix it — requires walking through the whole record.

How a Tax Ruling Became a Governance Problem

TWSD was established in 1992 to provide water, sanitation, and — according to its own website — road maintenance, a cemetery, a golf course, a swimming pool, and other recreational facilities to the roughly 9,000-acre community. That broad mandate ran on property tax revenue until 2006, when the Twelfth Judicial District Court ruled in Gambel v. TWSD that the Community Service District Act’s 10-mill property tax cap (NMSA 1978 §4-54-4) applied to water and sanitation districts. The ruling was certified as a final, appealable judgment. By the district’s own account to property owners, it cut TWSD’s tax revenue from roughly $364,000 to $134,000 a year — a loss of about $230,000 annually that had funded everything outside the water system itself.

Rather than shed those non-water services, the board voted in June 2012 to create a “Facilities and Services” (F&S) charge, billed to every property owner, explicitly to replace the lost tax revenue. The district’s own letter to residents that month said as much and itemized what the money would fund: road grading across 184 miles, the golf course, the pool, the cemetery, snow removal, trash hauling. That decision — replacing a capped tax with a new fee that funded the same non-water obligations — is the root of most of what has followed.

A District That’s Been Here Before

TWSD’s own public records include a “Final Receivership Order” and “Court Ordered Interim Rates” dating to around 2008 — meaning this is not the first time a court has had to step in and run the district’s water rates and operations from the bench. That history matters directly to the question of what happens next: a legal mechanism for placing TWSD under judicial receivership already exists, has already been used on this exact entity, and does not depend on resolving any of the newer legal questions raised by the community’s current governance-reform proposal.

Compliance Issues and Litigation, Piling Up

Since that 2012 fee was created, TWSD has accumulated an unusually dense litigation and regulatory record for a district serving roughly 600 households:

• PRC Docket 25-00011-UT (Mark Harding and Barbara Shockley) began over individual billing errors and expanded into a district-wide audit order. TWSD was ordered in December 2025 to audit its billing back to mid-2024 and prove it had issued required customer credits — a deadline extended once, to May 20, 2026. TWSD says it complied; both the complainants and the Commission itself said in late May that the proof submitted wasn’t sufficient. The docket remains open.

• PRC Docket 26-0000053 (Michael Gonzalez) argues the F&S fee is functioning as a disguised utility charge that should have required PRC approval — and, in a July 2026 filing, ties the fee’s 2012 origin directly to the 2006 tax judgment as evidence of a deliberate workaround. The PRC has not ruled on jurisdiction.

• At least eight Open Meetings Act complaints have been filed with the state Department of Justice since 2023. In November 2025, the DOJ found the board had “repeatedly violated” the Act, including improperly closing meetings under invalid claims of attorney-client privilege and disciplining an employee outside any public meeting. The agency’s deadlines — training by January 2026, cured violations reported back by May 2026 — have passed; no documentation confirming that reporting was found in the available record.

• An August 2024 letter from the district’s own law firm, Rodey, Dickason, Sloan, Akin & Robb, demanded $126,645.62 in unpaid legal invoices and threatened to withdraw from every pending case — including active litigation — if unpaid, while noting the firm’s own work had helped TWSD avoid “becoming insolvent or going into receivership” through a 2024 rate increase.

• A separate civil case, Massey v. Hanson and TWSD (Otero County District Court No. D-1215-CV-202500808), shows the district is already engaged in unrelated civil litigation in the same court that would have jurisdiction over any receivership petition.

None of these cases has produced a final resolution of TWSD’s underlying problems.

Each has instead documented another piece of the same pattern: financial strain, procedural noncompliance, and a board managing crises one complaint at a time.

The Present Crisis: Boiling Water, Broken Pipes, and a Hidden Violation

The district’s infrastructure problems are not new — a 2023 investigation found the system was losing approximately 85 percent of its treated water to leaks, much of it through thin-walled PVC pipe never rated for pressurized drinking water, with roughly half the community’s fire hydrants unusable. But the past several weeks have compounded that baseline failure. TWSD issued precautionary boil-water advisories on June 8, June 16, and July 8, 2026 — three in five weeks — each following a tank-pressure collapse. Board Chairman Otis Price has said the roughly 50-year-old system, built with substandard materials, is now failing faster than crews can repair it, citing close to 50 pipe breaks in a single month.

Separately, the New Mexico Environment Department issued a Notice of Violation on June 9, 2026, finding that TWSD failed to notify its own customers of an earlier drinking-water violation issued back in March — and failed to tell the state it had done so, as required within 10 days of any public notice going out.

NMED’s letter states the requirement was simply not met, and warns the district will now appear on the department’s public Enforcement Watch list, with NMED planning to notify local media directly. It is not the district’s only appearance there: NMED’s Resource Protection bureau has separately cited TWSD for operating an unregistered solid waste site since 1996.

A Golf Course for a Dollar a Month, a Pool That Never Opened

Against that backdrop, board minutes show TWSD approved a 10-year lease of its district-owned golf course and lounge building to a private operator, Discover Timberon Inc., for $1 a month — publicly noticed and voted 3–1 at an April 2025 meeting, with the district’s treasurer casting the dissenting vote over insurance concerns. Under the lease, the operator keeps 100 percent of profits while TWSD receives $12 a year and no revenue share, and no appraisal or market-rate comparison appears in the board’s own record of that vote — a gap that matters because New Mexico’s Anti-Donation Clause (N.M. Const. art. IX, §14) bars public bodies from giving away things of value to private parties without receiving fair consideration in return.

The same board separately voted, at that same meeting, to competitively bid a waste-management contract — showing it knew how to run a bid process when it used one.

Weeks later, TWSD announced the community pool — which lost roughly $26,500 against about $3,500 in revenue the prior summer — would not open for the season, citing a lack of funds and ongoing water concerns. 

Collecting From Ratepayers While the Taps Run Dry

The district’s most recent public board agenda, posted July 11, 2026, shows the board moving toward collections at the same time service is failing.

Item 5 approved 18 liens on standby lots totaling $4,430.10; item 6 proposed a “test” foreclosure against delinquent standby-fee accounts.

More than 200 properties are reportedly now eligible for foreclosure over unpaid fees, with the board having directed its attorney to review foreclosure options. Though historic documents show a procedure was previously in place thus why the need for a “test?

The same agenda proposed creating a leak-detection crew and expanding remote monitoring of the system — an implicit acknowledgment that neither exists yet in adequate form.

A prior board meeting’s own five-year capital plan ranked “Water System Replacement” as the district’s top infrastructure priority, alongside well rehabilitation and a new filtration unit — meaning the district’s own planning documents agree the core system needs rebuilding, even as ratepayers face collection action over bills owed to a utility currently under a boil-water advisory.

What Would Actually Fix This

Timberon’s former leadership has proposed a two-district governance model — leaving TWSD to focus solely on water while a new Community Service District, formed by Otero County, would take over roads, recreation, and the cemetery

That plan could potentially address the “mission creep” side of TWSD’s problems, but two things limit how quickly it could work.

First, it does not touch TWSD’s water infrastructure directly — the boil advisories, the pipe failures, and the NMED violations would remain TWSD’s to fix regardless of what happens to the golf course or the roads. 

Second, the specific state statute the plan cites for county authority to form the new district is a law governing narrow, single-project assessment districts, not standing multi-service governments — meaning the legal path for that half of the plan is not yet settled and would likely need further legal review, and possibly new state legislation, before a petition could be filed.

By comparison, a more direct and better-precedented path may already exists for the water system itself: judicial receivership, initiated by the PRC.

This is not a novel or untested idea for New Mexico’s small troubled water utilities — the PRC has pursued or discussed exactly this remedy in multiple recent cases, including a private utility in San Juan County and the Camino Real Regional Utility Authority in Sunland Park, both within the past year.

It is also not novel for TWSD specifically: the district’s own records show it was placed under a court-ordered receivership once before, around 2008, with a court setting interim rates during that period. A receivership would not require new legislation, would not depend on resolving the CSD’s open legal questions, and could be pursued through the existing PRC docket (25-00011-UT) already open against the district — the same docket a commissioner has already publicly floated receivership in.

Receivership would not by itself solve TWSD’s money problem — the district’s own former board chair has said the system needs $45 million to $50 million in infrastructure investment, and a receiver doesn’t bring new funding, only professional management and legal authority to act. But it would address the governance failures — the OMA violations, the undisclosed NMED violation, the golf course lease, the foreclosure push — by removing decision-making from an elected board that has, on the documented record, struggled to comply with its existing legal obligations. A parallel and non-exclusive option under New Mexico law is board removal through the courts under NMSA 1978 §73-21-12, with unfilled vacancies reverting to the district court under §73-21-13 — a slower, more democratic mechanism that residents can pursue directly without waiting on the PRC.

Realistically, the fastest and cleanest resolution likely combines pieces of both: PRC-driven receivership or court-supervised management to stabilize water operations immediately, alongside continued board-removal and ethics/records enforcement to address the accountability failures, with the community’s own CSD proposal — or an alternative legislative fix — addressing the non-water services on a longer timeline once the underlying legal question is resolved.

Why This Matters to Otero County

Timberon is unincorporated, which means Otero County has no direct governing authority over TWSD today — but the county is the body any new district would need to petition, and county residents and emergency responders bear real, immediate exposure to what happens in Timberon regardless of which government eventually runs it.

A water system that has lost the ability to reliably deliver water or verify its own test results is also a system that cannot reliably support fire suppression — a public-safety concern that doesn’t stop at Timberon’s boundary.

A district that cannot demonstrate the “Technical, Managerial, and Financial” capacity state and federal regulators require also cannot draw down the infrastructure funding that would otherwise fix the problem, leaving state and county resources as the more likely fallback the longer the current governance structure persists.

There is also a public trust question that outlasts any single lawsuits.

Twenty years of tax disputes, a fee created explicitly to work around a court order, repeated open-meetings violations, an undisclosed drinking-water violation, and a public asset leased away for a dollar a month are not, individually, unusual problems for a small rural utility to face. Together, and especially given that this district has already been through receivership once before, they describe an institution that has not demonstrated it can self-correct without outside intervention — which is precisely the finding that state regulators are now weighing whether to act on again.

This Alamogordo Town News article is part of  series and is based on a review of court orders, PRC filings, DOJ correspondence, board meeting records, IPRA responses, and reporting on the district’s current crisis, along with independent verification of the New Mexico statutes discussed. It is a factual summary, not legal advice. Where a fact could not be independently confirmed from the records reviewed, that limitation is noted directly in the text rather than presumed.

item.title: Alamogordo Police Report Multiple Arrests and Citations for July 6–12, 2026
item.description:
Alamogordo, NM — The Alamogordo Police Department responded to a variety of incidents during the week of July 6–12, 2026, resulting in numerous arrests, citations, and ongoing investigations. Charges included serious felonies such as criminal sexual penetration, aggravated battery, stalking, forgery, larceny, DWI, and drug-related offenses, along with several municipal violations.

Key categories of activity included:

• Domestic and Disturbance-Related Incidents: Multiple arrests for aggravated battery on a household member, disorderly conduct, resisting/evading/obstructing officers, breaking and entering, and stalking.

• Warrant Services: Numerous individuals were taken into custody on outstanding municipal, magistrate, and district court warrants for failure to appear, failure to pay, and other violations.

• DWI and Traffic Stops: Several arrests for driving while intoxicated, some involving additional charges.

• Property Crimes: Citations and arrests related to shoplifting, larceny, criminal damage to property, trespassing, and auto burglary.

• Drug and Other Offenses: Charges involving controlled substances, possession of paraphernalia, tampering with evidence, and related warrants. One case involved assistance with the White Mountain Drug Task Force leading to a methamphetamine trafficking warrant.

Most arrested individuals were booked into the Otero County Detention Center (OCDC) pending court appearances, while some received citations to appear or were released on their own recognizance or to courts.

No injuries to officers or major public safety incidents were highlighted in the logs.

item.title: In Memory of Louie Simon Jaramillo
item.description:
Oct 6, 1941 - Jul 5, 2026

Louie Simon Jaramillo, age 84, of Alamogordo, NM, passed away peacefully on July 5, 2026, in Albuquerque, NM.

Born on October 6, 1941, Louie lived a life defined by devotion to his family, hard work, and kindness. He shared 63 years of marriage with his wife, Irene Jaramillo. The two moved to Alamogordo in 1962 where Louie worked for NewTec out of White Sands Missile Range for over 52 years. Together, they built a home filled with love and cherished memories, where family was always at the center of their lives. Louie found his greatest joy in watching his sons and grandchildren play sports and traveling to all their games.

Louie was preceded in death by his parents, Louis O. Jaramillo and Edwina D. Jaramillo; and his brothers, Larry Jaramillo and Robert Jaramillo.

He is lovingly survived by his wife, Irene Jaramillo; his sons, Eugene Jaramillo (Maria), Roger Jaramillo, and Tony Jaramillo (Darian); his brothers, Norman Jaramillo (Claudette), Florencio Jaramillo (Clara), Kenneth Jaramillo (Elma), and Richard Jaramillo; his sisters, Marie Blea (Danny), Corrine Pino and sister-in-law, Carol Jaramillo. He also leaves behind many beloved nieces and nephews, all of whom held a special place in his heart.

Louie was a proud and loving grandfather to Lauren (Jon), Lucas, Audra, Adrienne (Josh), Taylor, and Lauren. He was also blessed with seven great-grandchildren, each of whom brought him immeasurable joy and pride.

Louie will be remembered for his love for his family, his generous heart, his quiet strength, and the wisdom he shared with those around him. Although his presence will be deeply missed, his memory will remain forever in the hearts of those who knew and loved him. His family finds comfort knowing that his love and guidance will continue to inspire them for many years.

A Funeral Mass celebrating Louie's life will be held on Saturday, August 1, 2026, at 11 a.m. at Our Lady of Sorrows Catholic Church in Cebolleta (Seboyeta), New Mexico. Family and friends are invited to attend and celebrate Louie's life. The Jaramillo family extends their heartfelt gratitude for the prayers, love, and support shown during this difficult time.

item.title: In Memory of Aylâ Hightower
item.description:
Jul 12, 1939 - Jun 26, 2026

Aylâ Hightower of Alamogordo, NM, passed away on June 26, 2026, at the age of 86. She was born on July 12, 1939, in Istanbul, Turkey, to Zehra Ener.

Aylâ immigrated to the United States as a young woman and married Richard Underwood in the late 1950's. The couple settled for a time in Lincoln, NE where they began raising their family. Together they had three children: Richard "Rick" Underwood, Tammy Underwood, and Wendy (Underwood) Muñiz.

In 1972, she opened Aylâ's Hair, Skin & Fine Fragrances at 1513 E. 10th Street in Alamogordo, where she lovingly served her clients for more than four decades before retiring in 2014. She was an exemplary businesswoman, tireless and exacting, who never compromised quality for convenience and set a standard few could match.

She later married Leroy Hightower in the late 1970's. Together they raised their grandchildren Brandon and Amber.

A woman of deep and steadfast faith, Aylâ was a devoted prayer warrior who prayed for anyone and everyone in need. She was known for her style, her candid outspokenness, and she never hesitated to advocate for the underdog and the less fortunate. A prolific writer, she published hundreds of articles on current affairs and on local and global politics, always in service of her community and the greater good. She was strikingly beautiful, the kind of beauty people remembered, and she carried that presence and style all her life.

Aylâ's home was a gathering place, and her table was its center. She was famous for her cooking, her börek especially, which disappeared as fast as she could make it; additionally, she was celebrated for a warmth that drew people in and never let them go. To more people than anyone could count, she was simply "Mom" and created a home teeming with life. She was, by every account, one of a kind, and those who knew her will not see anyone her like again.

Aylâ was preceded in death by her parents; her husband, Leroy; the father of her children, Richard Underwood; her daughter, Tammy Underwood; her grandson, Elijah Freedom Hightower; her son-in-law, Herbert Muñiz. She is survived by her children, grandchildren, and great grandchildren as well as their partners: Richard "Rick" Underwood and Laura Hawkins, Wendy Muñiz, Tammy Underwood's fiancée Freddy Padilla, Brandon and wife Rachel Hightower, Megan and husband Henry Valenzuela, Amber Underwood and fiancée Frank Stroehmer, Ayse Muñiz, Richard Muñiz and husband Gavin Williams, Dylan Muñiz and fiancée Amanda Townsend, Nikolas Valenzuela and fiancée Leilani Holt, Jeremiah Valenzuela, Rhiannon Valenzuela, Maximus Valenzuela, Xaniel Valenzuela, Kenzie Hightower and her fiancée Carson Martinez, Jeremiah D'Arezzo, Drake D'Arezzo, Julie D'Arezzo, Zeth Muñiz, Hadley Muñiz, Zayden Muñiz, and Lilly Muñiz, as well as a host of extended family, Glenn and Susie Underwood and their children Jason and Samantha. At the time of her passing, she was joyfully awaiting the arrival of her first great-great grandchild, expected later this year to Nikolas Valenzuela and Leilani Holt.

Services will be held at 11 a.m. on Saturday, August 1, 2026, at Christ Community Church. All members of the community impacted by Aylâ's life are encouraged to come.

item.title: Judge Sets Trial Date in Lawsuit Block Declared "Resolved" — Case Heads to Court in 2027
item.description:
Alamogordo NM- A 12th Judicial District Court judge has set a four-day civil trial for March 30 through April 2, 2027, in the lawsuit between state Rep. John P. Block IV and his former domestic partner — a case Block publicly declared "resolved amicably between the parties" 103 days ago, on his official Facebook page, as a sitting New Mexico state legislator.

Judge Lori L. Gibson Willard denied both of Block's motions for summary judgment at a July 13, 2026 hearing in Otero County, finding that breach-of-contract claims are viable and must proceed to trial. The ruling means the case — which Block characterized in an April 2, 2026 Facebook post as a settled "private property dispute" — will instead be decided by a judge after four days of testimony, evidence, and argument in early 2027. Far from "settled!"

Block, representing House District 51 in Alamogordo, is Ranking Minority Member of the House Consumer & Public Affairs Committee, the legislative panel with jurisdiction over consumer protection, debt collection, and lending regulation in New Mexico. He is represented by Albuquerque attorney Michael J. Seibel, who also operates Canvasback Financial Services LLC, a debt purchasing and receivables management firm regulated by the same consumer protection laws Block's committee oversees.

Block faces a contested race in the November 3, 2026 general election. Grace A. Nagamine, a lifelong Alamogordo resident and founder of Royal Angels, has qualified for the November ballot as an Independent candidate for House District 51. Nagamine filed her declaration of candidacy with the New Mexico Secretary of State, gathered the required nominating petition signatures, and met the petition filing deadline, qualifying her for the general election under New Mexico law. Her campaign committee — Grace for Neighbors Committee — is registered with the NM Secretary of State and listed as Compliant and Active, with a last filing date of July 7, 2026. Her platform focuses on veterans and Holloman Air Force Base, seniors and disability services, children and family welfare, homelessness and mental health, economic growth, and infrastructure. Nagamine's campaign website is graceforhd51.org. 

The April 2 Statement and What the Court Record Shows

On April 2, 2026, Block published a statement on his official Facebook page — identified as the public page of a sitting New Mexico state representative — stating: 'The lawsuit referenced in these posts has been mischaracterized. It was a private property dispute that has since been resolved amicably between the parties, and any claims otherwise are false.'

“The lawsuit referenced in these posts has been mischaracterized. It was a private property dispute that has since been resolved amicably between the parties, and any claims otherwise are false.”

— Rep. John P. Block IV — official Facebook page, April 2, 2026

The official court record tells a different story. As of the July 13, 2026 hearing, the case is set for trial, Block is listed in court documents as both Defendant and Counter-Plaintiff — meaning he has filed his own claims against Melton — and Judge Gibson Willard has ordered a scheduling order, commissioner appointment proceedings, and discovery to be completed before the March 2027 trial date.

Court records show the case number is D-1215-CV-2025-00757, filed in the 12th Judicial District Court, Otero County. Melton's breach-of-contract claim arises from the dissolution of their domestic partnership and a written agreement signed November 7, 2024, regarding shared property in Alamogordo.

What the Judge Ruled July 13

At the July 13 hearing, Judge Gibson Willard addressed multiple pending motions. Her rulings, as documented in the official court audio log:

JULY 13, 2026 RULINGS — JUDGE GIBSON WILLARD

First Motion for Summary Judgment: DENIED — Breach of contract claim regarding property removal survives; Melton has a right to the property or its value

Second Motion for Summary Judgment (re: loan, filed Dec. 19, 2025): DENIED — Court does not see how it can grant the motion

Discovery Motion (Melton's May 22 limited inspection request): DENIED on procedural grounds; attorney's fees question deferred to trial

Motion to Strike / Discovery Motion: GRANTED in part — specific motion struck and sealed on evidentiary grounds; case itself not sealed; future motions not sealed

Attorney's Fees (Seibel's sanctions request): DEFERRED to final hearing — not denied outright

Trial Date: SET — March 30 through April 2, 2027, four days, in person / Google Meet

Discovery: Scheduling order required; commissioner names due July 17, 2026

Commissioners: Must be independent; court will select from names submitted by parties

The denial of both summary judgment motions is a significant development. Summary judgment — which allows a court to resolve a case without trial when there are no genuine disputes of material fact — is typically Block's most powerful tool for ending the litigation short of a full hearing. Both attempts failed.

On the breach-of-contract claim, the judge found that while Block has a right to the items he removed from the shared residence, the breach-of-contract claim related to that removal survives and Melton has a right to the property or its equivalent value. That determination will be made at trial.

Block's Attorney: A Debt Collector Who Donated to His Campaign

Seibel, who has represented Block throughout the proceedings, is identified in court filings as 'Attorney for Defendant Block.' His law firm, Michael J. Seibel & Associates, is located at 8500 Menaul Blvd. NE, Suite A-410, Albuquerque. Court records confirm he has appeared on Block's behalf at multiple hearings from 2025 thru July 13, 2026.

Seibel's LinkedIn profile describes him as 'primarily handling collection of Personal and Business accounts' with 'over 20,000 collection matters and over 6,000 foreclosures.' He is the Managing Member of Canvasback Financial Services LLC, registered with the New Mexico Secretary of State in June 2022, which he describes as a 'receivables management firm operating in New Mexico... purchasing portfolios.'

Campaign finance records published by MoneyTrailNM.com — which draws data directly from the New Mexico Secretary of State's Campaign Finance Information System — show Seibel made two contributions to Block's campaign: $500.00 on December 30, 2021, and $156.15 on April 13, 2022, for a combined total of $656.15. Both contributions predated Block's assumption of office in January 2023.

A July 8, 2026 court filing by Melton — Plaintiff's Notice of Updated Repair Status and Continuing Preservation Issue — contains as Exhibit H an email chain between Melton and Seibel. The email chain shows Seibel conducting Block's legal defense communications from the email address mikecanvasback2014@___.com — a personal mail account bearing the name of his Canvasback Financial business.

“It no longer an emergency. We will figure it all out at the end of the case.”

— Michael J. Seibel — email to Karl Melton from mikecanvasback2014@___.com, July 6, 2026

Block has voted against every consumer protection bill that came before the House Consumer & Public Affairs Committee during the 2023, 2024, and 2025 legislative sessions. Official nmlegis.gov roll-call records document more than 14 such votes. Seibel's debt collection practice and Canvasback Financial's debt purchasing operations are directly regulated by the consumer protection framework that Block's committee oversees.

Block has made no public disclosure of the attorney-client relationship with Seibel, the campaign contributions, or any connection between the two relationships. ATN has requested confirmation from the New Mexico House of Representatives and the New Mexico Ethics Commission as to whether any disclosure was made through official channels. [

What the Court Sealed — and What It Didn't

At the July 13 hearing, Judge Gibson Willard granted Block's motion to strike and seal a specific filing — a May 22, 2026 Motion for Limited Discovery and Inspection, which had attached text communications as Exhibit A. The judge found the text messages were not appropriate attachments to a discovery motion.

The judge explicitly defined the scope of the sealing order from the bench: 'Not sealing entire case, not sealing future motions; just saying be careful what you attach.' The order applies to that specific motion and its exhibits. The case itself remains open and public. All other filings, including the June 23 Seibel motion and the July 8 and July 13 documents, remain in the public record.

“Not sealing entire case, not sealing future motions; just saying be careful what you attach.”

— Judge Lori L. Gibson Willard — July 13, 2026 hearing

The judge also noted at 10:42 a.m.: 'Would not allow these text messages to be in a pleading even if it wasn't Mr. Block who was an elected official' — indicating the ruling was based on evidentiary and procedural grounds applicable to any litigant, not on a finding that the underlying facts were false nor that prior reporting on the motion was improper.

ATN published reporting on the Discovery Motion and its contents before the sealing order was entered. Established First Amendment precedent holds that publication of information from public court records prior to a subsequent sealing order does not create liability for that prior publication. See United States v. Antar, 38 F.3d 1348 (3d Cir. 1994); Furgason v. Clausen, 109 N.M. 382 (N.M. Ct. App. 1989).

What Comes Next

Following the July 13 hearing, the case enters a formal discovery phase. The judge ordered a scheduling order to be submitted by the following week. Both parties were required to submit three names each for independent commissioners to be appointed to evaluate and potentially sell jointly-owned property; the judge indicated she would select from those names if not provided by July 17.

The trial is set for March 30 through April 2, 2027, at the 12th Judicial District Court in Alamogordo, with an option for Google Meet participation. The judge indicated the date will not be moved.

The attorney's fees question — Seibel's request for $5,000 in sanctions plus all fees and costs related to the discovery dispute — was deferred to the final hearing at trial and was not decided at the July 13 hearing. That issue remains open.

Background: A Lawsuit That Became a Broader Story

The Melton v. Block case has been the subject of reporting by ATN since fall 2025, based on records obtained through the New Mexico Inspection of Public Records Act and official court filings. ATN's prior coverage includes reporting on the filing of the lawsuit, the May 15, 2026 status hearing, the May 22, 2026 discovery motion, and Block's April 2, 2026 Facebook press release characterizing the case as resolved — a characterization the court record has consistently contradicted. Links to prior ATN coverage are available at AlamogordoTownNews.com.

The case has also been covered independently by Eddy and Lea County Exposed, a Facebook-based news and accountability publication serving Eddy and Lea counties in southeastern New Mexico with approximately 16,000 followers. That publication reported on the June 23, 2026 Seibel filing on July 1, 2026 — eight days after it was filed — under the headline 'Now Rep. John Block Wants the Court to Hide the Receipts?' Eddy and Lea County Exposed independently obtained the public court document and published its own analysis. ATN's coverage followed the same evening.

Eddy and Lea County Exposed has no documented connection to Melton, Edwards, or ATN. Its coverage was based entirely on the same public court record available to any member of the public or any journalist.

The legal threat in this matter has been directed exclusively at ATN and Edwards.

On April 2, 2026 — the same day Block published his 'resolved amicably' press release — Seibel transmitted a cease-and-desist letter to ATN and publisher Chris Edwards demanding removal of articles, cessation of further publication about Block, written retraction, identification of all confidential sources, and written confirmation of compliance within 10 days. 

As of publication date, no similar legal demand has been directed at Eddy and Lea County Exposed or any other publication that has covered the same court proceedings nor Block's record as a state representative.

item.title: Alamogordo Resident Kim White Owl Murillo Files Petition Seeking Recall of Commissioner Burnett
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO, N.M. — A city resident has filed a verified petition in state district court seeking a finding of probable cause to recall City Commissioner Stephen W. Burnett, citing his role in the ouster of the city’s former acting manager and the hiring of her successor.

Kim Murillo, a qualified elector of the City of Alamogordo and of District 2, filed the petition July 17 with the Twelfth Judicial District Court in Otero County. The case, No. D-1215-CV-2026-00626, has been assigned to Judge John P. Sugg. Murillo, who is representing herself, said the court waived the filing fee based on financial eligibility and will mail notice of a sufficiency hearing once it is scheduled.

Burnett was served through the City Clerk’s office at 4:09 p.m. the same day, according to Murillo, who said she retained On Point Courier & Legal Services to handle service.

What the petition alleges

The petition, brought under state law governing recalls in commission-manager cities, asks the court to determine there is probable cause to send recall grounds to voters based on conduct during Burnett’s current term, which began in January 2026 after his reelection to the District 2 seat.

Central to the filing is the Commission’s handling of the city manager’s post. According to the petition, the Commission voted 7–0 on March 10 to direct staff to negotiate a permanent contract with then-Acting City Manager Stephanie J. Hernandez, who had led the city for roughly 28 months and was, per the petition, the only candidate to pass the city’s scored interview process. A full contract was drafted but, the petition states, never finalized or offered to her.

Instead, the petition alleges that after a series of closed executive sessions, Burnett joined a 4–3 vote on April 28 to pay Hernandez and end her tenure rather than complete the March 10 agreement. The petition cites a city pay record showing a severance payment of $485,340.45 (net of $335,250) issued June 3, which Murillo says the Commission has not disclosed publicly.

The petition states this sum was proposed by Hernandez as compensation for simultaneously holding two roles for more than 20 months during the city’s manager search, not — as the petition specifically notes — a settlement tied to a separate EEOC charge she had filed as the investigation was never completed for an EEOC finding.

The petition further alleges that records obtained under the state’s public records law show the unfinished Hernandez contract was later revised into an agreement for Robert Stockwell, with his name inserted in place of hers and terms adjusted in his favor. Burnett voted June 23 to approve Stockwell’s hiring, according to the petition, even though Stockwell did not go through the same scored interview process applied to other candidates. That vote is cited in the petition as related to a pending Open Meetings Act lawsuit, Edwards v. Alamogordo City Commission, in which the district court recently allowed claims about the hiring to proceed to a hearing on the merits while denying a temporary restraining order.

The petition also raises a potential conflict of interest involving a pending $1 million economic development funding application from a business owned by Burnett’s sister-in-law. While Burnett recused himself from voting on the application, the petition alleges he continued to raise questions with the acting city manager about the funding process while it remained pending, and argues that conduct may run afoul of state ethics law regardless of the recusal.

Additionally, the petition states Burnett invited a constituent in February to submit questions about the city manager process but never substantively responded to them.

Based on these allegations, the petition asks the court to find probable cause for recall on grounds of misfeasance, malfeasance, and violation of Burnett’s oath of office. A city ordinance and the city’s code of conduct assign day-to-day administrative authority to the city manager rather than individual commissioners, the petition notes, and cites the departing acting manager’s June 9 public remarks describing a pattern of commissioners bypassing that office.

These are allegations contained in a court filing; they have not been ruled on by a judge, and Burnett has not yet had the opportunity to respond in court.

Murillo was interviewed following the filing by WalkerTown News on Facebook and by Anthony Lucero of KALH Radio.

WalkerTown News interview with Kim Murillo: https://www.facebook.com/share/v/1EqdfuU4Pk/?mibextid=wwXIfr

Alamogordo Town News streaming on KALH Radio interview with Anthony Lucero: https://youtu.be/3GcAnLBQ7ek?is=ZSFje56mpuR_4ZHf

Next steps

Under the process described in the petition, a district court hearing will determine whether probable cause exists before any recall petition can be circulated for signatures. Murillo said she is coordinating with other volunteers, including a separate recall effort targeting Commissioner Baxter Pattillo, and is seeking additional petition circulators in Districts 4 and 5. She said she plans to share hearing details, including whether remote access will be available, once the court issues notice.

This article is based on a verified petition filed in the Twelfth Judicial District Court and statements provided by the petitioner

The allegations contained in the petition are up to the court to decide if it merits a recall effort petition effort of the voters. Commissioner Burnett has not yet responded in the litigation effort nor filed a public comment upon being served.

item.title: City of Alamogordo and Alamogordo MainStreet Invite Community to HAWK Launch Party August 8
item.description:
Alamogordo, NM — Come out and celebrate a major step forward for pedestrian safety in downtown Alamogordo at the HAWK Launch Party on Saturday, August 8, 2026, from 4 p.m. to 8 p.m. at the intersection of E. 10th Street and New York Avenue.

The event, hosted by the City of Alamogordo and Alamogordo MainStreet, will mark the activation of the city’s first High-Intensity Activated Crosswalk (HAWK) signal — also known as a Pedestrian Hybrid Beacon (PHB). This new traffic safety feature is designed to better protect pedestrians and visitors in the downtown area.

How the HAWK Signal Works

The HAWK system remains dark when not in use, allowing normal traffic flow. When a pedestrian pushes the button:

• Flashing yellow lights warn drivers.

• A steady yellow light follows.

• Then a solid red light requires vehicles to stop.

After the red phase, the lights flash red, allowing drivers to proceed with caution once the crossing is clear of pedestrians. When the lights go dark again and the intersection is clear, normal traffic resumes. This innovative beacon improves safety without unnecessary delays for vehicles.

For the launch party, New York Avenue will be closed from 9th Street to 10th Street, and 10th Street will be closed from Delaware Avenue to the vicinity of the crossing.

Family-Friendly Fun for All Ages

The afternoon and evening celebration will feature something for everyone:

• Meet the Holly Hawk Mascot!

• Classic Car Show

• Dunk Tank

• Beer Garden

• Food Trucks

• Free Hot Dogs (first 300 guests)

The event is free and open to the public, making it a perfect opportunity for families, downtown visitors, and the entire community to gather, enjoy live entertainment, and see the new safety improvement in action.

This new pedestrian signal represents the City’s ongoing commitment to improving safety and vitality in the downtown district. Alamogordo MainStreet continues to work hand-in-hand with city officials to create welcoming public spaces that encourage foot traffic and community engagement.

Mark your calendar and join the celebration on Saturday, August 8, 2026, from 4–8 p.m. at E. 10th Street & New York Avenue. Bring the family, show off your ride, enjoy great food and drinks, and help welcome Alamogordo’s first HAWK pedestrian crossing!

item.title: In Memory of Lorene Merrick
item.description:
Lorene Merrick, born June 16, 1951, passed away surrounded by the love of those she held dear. She was a devoted mother, sister, and friend whose warmth and humor touched countless lives.

Lorene had a special love for her family, her sons, and even their beloved pets, who were always part of her extended circle of care. She often joked that she and her three sisters were like the “Golden Girls,” a bond filled with laughter, loyalty, and lifelong friendship.

Known for her playful spirit, Lorene loved clowning around and bringing smiles to others. Her ability to make people laugh was one of her greatest gifts, and she shared it freely. She also cherished her many friendships, holding each one close to her heart.

A cancer survivor, Lorene showed strength and resilience throughout her life, inspiring those around her with her courage and faith.
Today, we find comfort in knowing she is at peace, reunited with Jesus and the loved ones who preceded her. Though she will be deeply missed, we celebrate her life and the joy she brought into ours, holding her memory in our hearts always.

item.title: Tularosa Basin Downwinders Consortium Hosts 17th Annual Candlelight Vigil for Trinity Test Victims
item.description:
Tularosa, NM – The Tularosa Basin Downwinders Consortium (TBDC) will hold its 17th Annual Candlelight Vigil on Saturday, July 25, 2026, to remember those lost to cancer and honor survivors impacted by radioactive fallout from the 1945 Trinity atomic bomb test.

On July 16, 1945, the United States detonated the world’s first atomic device at the Trinity Site in the Tularosa Basin. The blast and subsequent radioactive fallout exposed residents in nearby communities — including Tularosa, Alamogordo, and surrounding areas in Otero, Lincoln, Socorro, and Sierra counties — to dangerous levels of radiation without warning or adequate protection. Decades later, families continue to experience disproportionately high rates of cancer, birth defects, and other radiation-related illnesses. The TBDC, founded in 2005 by Tina Cordova and the late Fred Tyler, was established to document these health impacts, compile survivor stories, and advocate for justice and compensation for what advocates call the “unknowing, unwilling, and uncompensated” victims of America’s nuclear age.

The vigil will take place at the Tularosa Veterans Memorial Park, 901 North Bookout, Tularosa, NM 88352. Gates will open at 7:30 p.m., with the program starting at 8:00 p.m. Attendees will join a solemn candlelight tribute.

Mayors from Tularosa and Alamogordo are expected to attend and speak at the event, underscoring local government support for the downwinders’ cause and the importance of community remembrance and advocacy.

Luminarias honoring loved ones who lost their battle with cancer will be available for a suggested donation of $1.00 each.

TBDC members will provide information on the Radiation Exposure Compensation Act (RECA) and guidance on how to apply. An update on the RECA program — expanded in recent years to include Trinity downwinders — will also be presented. Many families have now received compensation, but advocates emphasize the need for continued outreach to ensure eligible individuals are supported.

For more information, contact Tina Cordova at 505-897-6787 or tcordova@queston.net. Visit www.trinitydownwinders.com for additional details.

The annual vigil serves as both a memorial and a call to action, highlighting the human cost of the Trinity test and the ongoing fight for full recognition and support for affected New Mexico families. The public is warmly invited to attend.

item.title: Doña Ana County Board of Commissioners Terminates County Manager Scott Andrews’ Contract

Las Cruces, NM – The Doña Ana County Board of Commissioners unanimously voted Tuesday, July 21, 2026, to terminate the employment contract of County Manager Scott Andrews, effective immediately.

The special meeting agenda, which included a possible closed session to discuss “a limited personnel matter related to the County Manager,” led to the unanimous decision in open session. Andrews was terminated without cause. Per the terms of his contract and a signed separation agreement, he will receive six months of salary.

County officials stated that the Board will now focus on determining next steps for leadership. Additional information will be shared with the public as it becomes available.

Andrews’ Background

Scott Andrews was appointed County Manager on August 13, 2024, by the Doña Ana County Board of Commissioners. At the time of his hiring, the county highlighted his more than 21 years of experience in public sector administration. Andrews brought extensive expertise in:

• Economic development

• Quality of life initiatives

• Community relations

• Consensus building

• Modernization of municipal organizations

His termination comes less than two years into his tenure.

The agenda for the special meeting held at 2:30 p.m. in the Doña Ana County Government Center (845 North Motel Boulevard, Las Cruces) followed standard protocol, including invocation, Pledge of Allegiance, and roll call, before addressing the personnel matter.

This leadership change affects one of southern New Mexico’s largest counties, which serves a diverse and growing population along the U.S.-Mexico border. The Board of Commissioners has not yet announced an interim manager or a timeline for a permanent replacement.

Alamogordo Town News will continue monitoring developments and provide updates as more information is released by the county

What Was Facebook Announcement Is Now Reality: Independent Candidate Roderick Saint Officially Removed from November General Election Ballot.

Following up on independent candidate Roderick Saint’s initial withdrawal announcement posted to Facebook on July 13, 2026,  as previously reported by Alamogordo Town News, the withdrawal is now official.

Geraldine Yazza Martinez Responds

“Yesterday, my campaign team obtained official documentation confirming that Mr. Saint filed the necessary paperwork to withdraw his candidacy and be removed from the November General Election ballot,” Martinez stated.

The resolution is comprehensive

“With this matter resolved, my focus remains on serving the Village of Tularosa as your Chief of Police while continuing to prepare for the opportunity to serve all of Otero County as your next Sheriff,” she said.

Background: A Troubled Campaign for Saint

Saint’s path to the ballot had been rocky from the outset. Martinez’s campaign challenged the validity of his nominating petition signatures, which he had submitted with 406 names against a requirement of 353. The review reportedly found duplicate signatures, incomplete entries, and illegible information.

On July 13, 2026, Saint announced his withdrawal via Facebook, citing “two unexpected personal losses” and stating that his family’s well-being required him to step aside.

The 41-year law enforcement veteran said he was proud of his career and needed time to focus on his family’s healing and recovery.

In that same announcement, however, Saint criticized what he characterized as attacks against him “even before I qualified to be on the ballot,” and suggested he would release documents regarding Martinez’s law enforcement background, though he provided no documentation with his announcement.

Martinez’s Vision and Response

“I sincerely wish Mr. Saint and his family the very best during this next chapter of their lives. They will be in my thoughts and prayers,” she said.

Moving Forward to November

The resolution eliminates what could have been a prolonged legal distraction, allowing Martinez to focus on her campaign and connecting with voters. Though Martinez now faces an essentially unopposed race, she has made clear she intends to earn every vote.

“While there is now only one election remaining, I will not take a single vote for granted. I respectfully ask for your support in November as we continue working toward a Sheriff’s Office built on justice, accountability, and public trust,” Martinez said.

She also expressed gratitude for the support her campaign has received throughout this period.

“I am grateful for the overwhelming support my campaign has received,” Martinez stated.

The Otero County Sheriff’s election is scheduled for November, with Martinez’s vision centered on the three principles she has consistently emphasized: justice, accountability, and public trust.

“I am looking forward to serving the people of Otero County and earning their trust through honesty and professionalism,” Martinez concluded.

item.title: The right information can change everything
item.description:
By Chief Justice Julie J. Vargas

As Chief Justice, one of my priorities is to ensure that access to justice is not just an abstract ideal, but a reality for the people of our state. Nearly half of all newly filed civil cases in district courts in the past three fiscal years involved at least one party who represented themselves without an attorney.

To assist people in navigating the state court system, the Judiciary has launched a critical new resource: the New Mexico Courts HelpLine at (855) 268-7804.

The HelpLine expands access to justice by connecting callers directly with trained court experts whose sole focus is providing direction to those who represent themselves in court and individuals with questions about a legal matter. It is important to clarify that the HelpLine’s staff cannot provide legal advice, and they cannot act as your attorney. However, what these court experts do provide is accurate, reliable guidance on court case procedures. They guide callers directly to the correct state court forms, explaining the specific rules for filing or responding to lawsuits, and point folks to legal aid services across the state.

Providing this clear direction is essential. A single toll-free call to these court experts can help people make informed decisions. Anxiety about the unknown is often worse than the reality. By replacing uncertainty with clarity, we give self-represented litigants the solid footing they need to walk into a courthouse prepared.

Access to justice also means meeting New Mexicans where they are. The HelpLine is entirely free and open to all residents. Whether you live in Alamogordo, Farmington, Las Cruces, Gallup, or Roswell, you no longer have to drive to a courthouse to find someone who can explain court procedures. Our staff is fully bilingual in Spanish, with interpreters available for Diné and other languages. Because working families cannot always call during regular business hours, our experts are available six days a week — Monday through Friday from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m., and Saturday from 9 a.m. to 1 p.m.

If your situation ultimately requires formal legal representation, our experts will also help connect you with low- and no-cost legal aid organizations or upcoming free legal fairs.

If you are staring at the ceiling tonight, worrying about a pending court case, you do not have to figure it out by yourself. Stop guessing and reach out to the New Mexico Courts HelpLine.

Help is available at (855) 268-7804. Let us help you take your first step in navigating the courts.

That's how you empower people!  Happy to see that added here, much needed.

item.title: RPNM Must Stop the Torrance County Reorganization Until It Follows Its Own Rules By Gary Person
item.description:
RPNM’s proposed reorganization of the Republican Party of Torrance County should be suspended immediately.

The issue is not personalities. It is authority.

RPNM issued a July 20, 2026 call for a “Biennial Organizational County Convention” to elect a new County Central Committee, county officers, and SCC contingent.

But USR 3-2-1(C) places the Biennial Organizational County Convention in odd-numbered years. It is the convention used to elect precisely those positions.

2026 is not an odd-numbered year.

RPNM relies on USR 2-1-4(F)(7), but that rule is a limited remedy allowing the state chairman to call a regularly required organizational convention when a county fails or refuses to hold it. It does not expressly authorize RPNM to terminate existing terms, remove an entire county organization, or create an additional organizational election in an even-numbered year.

The SCC Did Not Adjudicate the Case

USR 2-1-2(D) gives the State Central Committee authority to act when it finds that a county caucus, convention, or election was improperly held or not held.

The Torrance County matter was placed on the SCC agenda, but the June 20 meeting did not reach quorum.

Therefore, the SCC did not make findings, approve removals, or authorize a complete county reorganization at that meeting.

A memorandum titled “Issue for the SCC to consider” is not an SCC ruling. It lists allegations involving resignations, residency, finances, records, and the closure of the county bank account, but it does not constitute a vote or adjudication.

The Executive Committee, Executive Director Leticia Muñoz, and Mark Van Dyke cannot substitute their judgment for an SCC decision unless they can produce a valid rule or recorded SCC delegation authorizing them to do so.

No Lawful Removal Process Has Been Shown

The USRs require specific procedures to remove county officers, County Central Committee members, and SCC contingent members. Those procedures generally require:

RPNM should produce the notices, quorum records, motions, vote totals, and minutes showing that these procedures were followed.

Until then, it should not act as though the entire Torrance County organization has already been lawfully removed.

Vacancies Do Not Erase the County Party

Even if several county offices are vacant, the rules provide methods for filling vacancies. They do not state that vacancies automatically dissolve the County Central Committee or cancel every existing SCC position.

USR 3-1-1 identifies the County Central Committee as the governing body of the Republican Party within the county.

RPNM must follow the vacancy and removal rules before replacing the entire organization.

RPNM Must Account for Torrance County’s Money and Property

RPNM’s own document states that the Torrance County bank account was closed on March 4, 2026.

Torrance County officials further allege that funds were removed by the former treasurer and that RPNM is retaining county money, records, or property.

Those allegations require an immediate written accounting stating:

According to Leanne Tapia, Mark Van Dyke told her that the only way Torrance County could “get back to work” was to hold the proposed election.

Tapia also sent a written notice disputing RPNM’s factual basis for the reorganization, requesting cancellation of the meeting, and asking RPNM to identify the rule authorizing it. Van Dyke was copied on that correspondence.

If the county’s money, records, property, or ability to operate are being conditioned on participation in the disputed election, RPNM should immediately withdraw that condition.

County assets should not be used as leverage in an internal political dispute.

Leticia Muñoz Previously Recognized the County’s Records

In 2024, Leticia Muñoz asked whether the Torrance County Central Committee had voted to approve two SCC members. After receiving confirmation, she replied, “Awesome! Thanks Betty!”

RPNM’s later records also listed Torrance County officers and SCC members.

Those records may require review, but they undermine any suggestion that RPNM never recognized a functioning Torrance County organization.

The Rules Apply to RPNM Leadership Too

USR 1-5-2 states that the Uniform State Rules apply throughout the state and cannot be suspended at either the state or county level.

Judge Cindy M. Mercer expressed the same principle in the Amy Barela litigation:

“By voluntarily joining the party, Defendants agreed to be bound by its bylaws.”

That principle applies equally to the Executive Committee, Leticia Muñoz, Mark Van Dyke, and every other RPNM official.

What RPNM Should Do

RPNM should:

Until that occurs, RPNM has not demonstrated lawful authority to replace the entire Torrance County Republican organization.

Return the county’s property.
Stop obstructing its work.
Let the SCC decide the dispute.
Follow the rules.

item.description:
Service members from Holloman Air Force Base recently rolled up their sleeves on New York Avenue, painting a vibrant new mural and refreshing an overhang as part of the base’s Big Give community service effort.

Airmen from the 54th Operations Support Squadron completed the project, contributing to ongoing revitalization in Alamogordo’s historic downtown. The Big Give is a month-long initiative in which Holloman squadrons partner with local communities across Otero County to restore and improve public and commercial spaces. Officials describe the effort as service beyond the mission that strengthens ties between the base and the surrounding area.

The work comes amid continued private business investment in the New York Avenue corridor. Alamogordo MainStreet has advanced infrastructure and streetscape improvements on the 800 and 900 blocks in recent years, including utilities upgrades, sidewalks, lighting, and public art that aim to make the district more inviting for residents and visitors.

New businesses are also adding momentum. The Drink Well, Alamogordo’s first dirty soda shop, opened inside the Ink Well Innovation Center at 314 E. 9th Street. The shop serves creative dirty sodas, energy drink concoctions, snacks, and signature “inks.” Hours are 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. Monday through Friday. The Ink Well itself was developed to support local entrepreneurship and small-business growth, providing a fitting home for the new venture. A grand opening was held June 17.

A short walk away on New York Avenue, Pink Flamingo Funky Finds opened its doors at 900 New York Ave. in early July. The shop specializes in unique gifts, vintage items, handmade goods, and one-of-a-kind finds. Its arrival coincided with Downtown Nites activities that draw shoppers, food vendors, music, and community foot traffic to the district.

Together, the volunteer improvements by Holloman personnel and the arrival of new independent retailers underscore a broader push to keep downtown Alamogordo lively and welcoming. Local leaders and MainStreet advocates continue to encourage residents to support these businesses, explore the refreshed streetscape, and take part in the community spaces that result from partnerships like the Big Give.

Visitors can find both shops and the latest mural work along the New York Avenue corridor in the heart of downtown.

item.title: Gaming Board Shuts Down Ruidoso Track; Businesses Expect 35-40% Revenue Drop
item.description:
New Mexico facility faces prolonged closure due to flood damage; Ruidoso prepares for significant economic downturn

RUIDOSO DOWNS, N.M. — The New Mexico Gaming Control Board unanimously approved the suspension of Ruidoso Downs Race Track and Casino operations this week, marking the third consecutive summer the facility has been forced to close due to flood damage from last year’s Salt and South Fork fires.

Heavy flooding left the culvert at the track’s main entrance badly damaged, prompting the New Mexico Department of Transportation to recommend suspending all casino and race simulcast operations for safety reasons.

The track adds $160-180 million a year in revenue to the region’s economy, making this closure a critical blow to the area. The timing is particularly damaging, hitting during peak summer weekends when regular patrons typically stay multiple weeks enjoying the racing events and contributing directly to local hospitality businesses.

“That is a real big jewel in the crown that is Ruidoso so we have to get them back,” said Lynn Crawford, Mayor of the Village of Ruidoso, adding that the impact extends beyond just the track itself. “A lot of those folks that come in for the track to go to the races every weekend, that stay here for 3 or 4 weeks out of the year, people that work at the track. We’re really feeling it big time.”

Partial Operations and Recovery Efforts

The facility will continue to host its quarter horse and thoroughbred sales, as well as the All American Select sale, at the sales pavilion. The track previously moved its horse racing schedule to Albuquerque to maintain some operations despite the closure.

To combat the economic downturn, the Mescalero Apache Tribe is leveraging its portfolio of regional enterprises. The tribe operates Inn of the Mountain Gods Resort & Casino, Ski Apache, and Casino Apache Travel Center, providing alternative attractions to keep visitors in the region during the track’s closure.

The 273-room Inn of the Mountain Gods offers live music, horseback riding, golf, big game hunting, fishing and kayak rentals, along with a 38,000 square-foot casino featuring Las Vegas-style gaming. During summer, Ski Apache operates the Apache Arrow high-speed gondola to the Sierra Blanca summit and rents mountain bikes and disc golf equipment.

The tribe also operates the 50,000-square-foot Casino Apache Travel Center on U.S. 70, featuring a convenience store, restaurant, smoke shop, gas station and truck stop services, positioning these businesses as economic lifelines during the extended closure.

Looking Forward

Mayor Crawford expressed confidence that the track would eventually reopen once mitigation efforts are complete. “Crawford said that they’re confident the track will reopen once mitigation efforts are complete,” according to recent statements.

In the meantime, the community is relying on diversified tourism attractions, including Ruidoso’s unique shops, dining establishments, and outdoor recreation opportunities, combined with the Mescalero Apache Tribe’s resort and entertainment enterprises to weather the economic storm.

For residents and business owners who have already endured three years of track closures, the path to full recovery remains uncertain. The region’s economic resilience will depend on the pace of infrastructure repairs and the ability of alternative attractions to maintain visitor interest during this extended closure period.

item.title: Alamogordo Police Department Reports Varied Criminal Activity During July 13-19
item.description:
Alamogordo — The Alamogordo Police Department’s weekly activity log for July 13-19, 2026, documented a range of criminal incidents across the community, including drug-related charges, theft, domestic violence, and traffic violations.

Violent Crimes and Domestic Incidents

Multiple domestic violence cases were reported during the week. Officers responded to battery and assault incidents involving household members, resulting in arrests and court proceedings. One aggravated assault case involving a deadly weapon was documented, with ongoing investigations continuing through the week.

A shots-fired incident was reported in the Indian Wells and Florida area on Friday, with several suspects taken into custody as the investigation remained ongoing.

Drug-Related Offenses

Law enforcement conducted operations in coordination with the White Mountain Drug Task Force, leading to multiple arrests for controlled substance possession and related violations. Cases included possession of methamphetamine, cocaine, and drug paraphernalia. Several individuals were charged with trafficking controlled substances and failure to comply with conditions of release related to prior drug offenses.

Theft and Property Crimes

The week saw multiple theft incidents, including shoplifting cases at local retail establishments. A residential burglary on South Linda Vista resulted in the theft of a gun safe containing firearms and cash, with no signs of forced entry. Investigators documented breaking and entering, larceny, and criminal damage to property charges in connection with the incident.

Additional property crimes included unauthorized use of public property, criminal damage charges, and cases involving stolen property disposition.

Traffic Violations and Accidents

Two vehicle crashes with injuries were reported—one involving a Toyota Camry and Chevrolet Trailblazer at US Highway 70 and US Highway 54, and another involving a motorcycle on New York Avenue at First Street. Drivers reported minor injuries, with one motorcyclist transported to an area hospital with non-life-threatening injuries.

Multiple DWI arrests were made following traffic stops, along with failure-to-pay-fines citations and other traffic-related violations.

Warrant Enforcement and Court Issues

Officers made numerous arrests on outstanding municipal and magistrate court warrants for failure to appear and failure to pay fines. These enforcement actions resulted in several individuals being incarcerated pending court proceedings and bond hearings.

Regulatory Violations

Cases were documented for animal control violations, including an animal at large and vaccine requirement case. Code enforcement issues included citations for international property maintenance violations, unlawful growth or accumulation on lots, and park closure hours violations.

Other Incidents

One unattended death was investigated on Sunday, involving a 78-year-old female found inside a residence. Medical examiners and detectives determined the cause of death appeared to be from natural causes.

Juvenile offenses included a runaway report and battery referrals to the Juvenile Probation Officer.

item.title: New Mexico Claims Federal Government Broke 2019 Epstein Investigation Agreement
item.description:
Santa Fe — The New Mexico Department of Justice is escalating its dispute with the federal government over access to unredacted Epstein investigation files, with former Attorney General Hector Balderas now publicly confirming details of an alleged 2019 prosecutorial agreement that he says the federal government has failed to honor.

The 2019 Agreement

According to correspondence released by the state, Balderas’s office and the Southern District of New York (SDNY) reached an explicit agreement in mid-2019 regarding separate investigations into Jeffrey Epstein’s Zorro Ranch property in New Mexico.

The agreement allegedly stipulated that New Mexico’s AG office would suspend its independent investigation and interviews with victims, while turning over materials gathered to federal prosecutors. In exchange, SDNY committed to referring any state-related matters uncovered during its investigation back to New Mexico once its case concluded.

“New Mexico honored its side of an agreement with the federal government, and the federal government did not honor its own,” said current Attorney General Raúl Torrez in a statement. “That breach doesn’t weaken our position, it strengthens it. New Mexico is entitled to these records.”

The Timeline of Investigation and Dispute

New Mexico’s investigation into Epstein and the Zorro Ranch property began in early 2019. By mid-2019, state investigators had located and begun formally interviewing victims with potential knowledge of criminal conduct at the property—work conducted in parallel with the emerging federal investigation.

When Epstein was arrested on federal sex trafficking charges on July 6, 2019, SDNY contacted state officials. The agency initially expressed frustration that state investigators were interviewing witnesses SDNY considered part of its federal investigation.

Balderas cited a handwritten investigator’s note released under the Epstein Files Transparency Act (EFTA01681971) as documentation of the agreement’s terms.

Recent Escalation of Demands

The current dispute between state and federal authorities spans several months:

• In February 2026, New Mexico sent written correspondence to the U.S. Department of Justice requesting access to specific materials and all Zorro Ranch investigative documents.

• By March 2026, the state had submitted a formal letter identifying five illustrative redacted documents and requesting complete, unredacted versions.

• In May 2026, New Mexico submitted a formal “Touhy letter” through standard legal channels requesting the materials.

• Despite multiple follow-ups and a request for an in-person meeting in June, federal officials did not provide substantive responses.

On June 9, 2026, Attorney General Torrez sent a detailed letter to acting federal officials outlining the 2019 agreement and seeking broad remedies, including forfeiture of the Zorro Ranch property.

Federal Response Falls Short

On July 10, 2026, the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of New Mexico delivered its response: 31 pages consisting almost entirely of documents already released through public EFTA channels, heavily redacted materials offering no new investigative content, and photocopies of local news coverage.

The production did not include the comprehensive, unredacted investigative record New Mexico had requested.

After an attempt to contact SDNY representatives on July 13 produced no results, New Mexico issued a final written demand on July 14, setting a deadline of July 31, 2026 for full access to unredacted materials.

Next Steps

Torrez warned in his correspondence that absent compliance by the deadline, New Mexico will treat the request as denied and pursue all available legal remedies. The state has signaled its willingness to pursue litigation to compel the release of the materials.

“We will use every tool available, including litigation, to obtain them,” Attorney General Torrez stated.
