item.title: From Personal Lawsuit to Accountability Journalism: How One Civil Rights Case Sparked a Movement Exposing Eddy County Corruption
item.description:
Roswell — What began as a single lawsuit against Eddy County officials has evolved into a grassroots accountability movement with more than 16,000 followers documenting alleged political corruption and Inspection of Public Records Act (IPRA) violations. The plaintiff, wrongfully prosecuted and incarcerated according to court records and personal statements, initially created an online presence to document their own case. When reports from others with similar experiences began flooding in—stories of citizens being ignored, silenced, wrongfully charged, and intimidated—the effort transformed into something larger.

“When I started this page, it was about getting justice for what happened to me. Then I started hearing your stories,” the plaintiff wrote. “That is when this became bigger than me.”

Now, as the case heads toward a critical settlement conference on September 18, 2026, the accountability journalism organization continues to shed light on patterns of alleged abuse within Eddy County’s justice system. The movement emphasizes its independence from traditional power structures: “I do not have political connections. I do not have status. I do not have powerful people protecting me. I am not riding anyone’s coattails.”

The Legal Framework: IPRA, Qualified Immunity, and Accountability

Central to the movement is New Mexico’s Inspection of Public Records Act (IPRA)—a tool the organization uses to expose alleged governmental misconduct. By documenting instances where agencies fail to provide public records or obstruct transparency, the movement builds evidence of institutional resistance to accountability.

The plaintiff argues that IPRA violations work in concert with prosecutorial misconduct and qualified immunity to shield officials from consequences. Qualified immunity—a legal doctrine that shields government officials from civil liability unless they violated a “clearly established” constitutional right—has historically insulated officials from personal liability, even when their conduct was allegedly unlawful.

The underlying lawsuit (Case No. 25-226 MIS/GJF) names Michael Gallagher and the Eddy County Board of Commissioners as defendants and involves claims under 42 U.S.C. § 1983, which provides remedies for constitutional violations committed under color of state law. The movement contends that absent accountability mechanisms, these protections become tools to enable abuse.

September 18: A Test of Institutional Power

The settlement conference, scheduled for 10:00 a.m. MDT on Friday, September 18, 2026, at the United States District Court in Roswell, has become a symbolic focal point for the 16,000-follower movement. The plaintiff views it as a test of whether ordinary citizens can successfully challenge institutional power that has historically insulated government officials from consequences.

“On September 18, I’ll be walking back into the same judicial district that prosecuted me and where I was wrongfully incarcerated—this time standing up for my constitutional rights,” the plaintiff wrote, framing the moment as emblematic of a larger struggle.

According to the court order filed July 22, 2026, all parties and their lead trial counsel are required to appear in person with “full and final authority” to discuss binding settlement options. The plaintiff has called for peaceful public presence outside the courthouse that day and specifically named Fifth Judicial District Attorney Diana Luce, Lea County Sheriff’s Office, and other public officials as representatives of the accountability issues the movement addresses.

A Movement Beyond One Case

The accountability organization has become a repository for public complaints about prosecutorial overreach and IPRA violations—transforming individual grievances into documented evidence of systemic patterns. With 16,000 followers, the movement has established itself as a force for governmental transparency in Eddy County, attracting attention from citizens and observers interested in the intersection of qualified immunity with aggressive prosecutorial tactics.

“This fight was meant to show everyone that you can stand your ground—even when people laugh at you, mock you, belittle you, and tell you that you will never win,” the plaintiff stated, describing the larger significance the movement now carries.

Regardless of the outcome on September 18, the organization plans to continue monitoring official conduct, documenting alleged IPRA violations, and amplifying the experiences of those who believe they have been subjected to prosecutorial misconduct. The settlement conference represents a critical juncture, but it is not an endpoint. Federal rules require good faith settlement negotiations; if no agreement is reached, the case will proceed toward trial.

The IPRA Task Force: A Critical Moment for Transparency

As the accountability movement gains traction, New Mexico’s IPRA Task Force is currently traveling the state to discuss the Inspection of Public Records Act and its implementation. The timing is significant—and contested.

According to the accountability organization and allied independent media outlets such as AlamogordoTownNews.org, government officials have attempted to weaponize the IPRA process itself, using procedural restrictions and hostile interpretations of the law to close down records requests and obstruct the transparency mechanisms designed to hold officials accountable. This approach effectively reverses IPRA’s purpose: rather than ensuring public access to records, officials have exploited technicalities and compliance burdens to deny access.

“When government uses IPRA procedures and noncompliance as a weapon to prevent transparency rather than facilitate it, they undermine the very foundation of accountability,” claims IPRA advocate, Chris Edwards

Multiple independent news organizations view the task force’s statewide tour as a critical opportunity to educate the public about IPRA’s essential role in democratic oversight and to counteract attempts to weaken public access by government officials and bureaucrats. 

Public Comment: Your Voice Matters

This accountability organization, alongside Eddy and Lea County Exposed and other independent media organizations, and other statewide transparency advocates, is urging the public to submit formal comments supporting IPRA and its critical role in holding government accountable. Public comment periods represent one of the few direct mechanisms citizens have to influence policy discussions occurring at the state level.

Citizens are encouraged to submit comments emphasizing:

• IPRA’s essential role in government accountability and transparency

• Examples of government obstruction of public records requests

• The importance of maintaining strong IPRA protections against erosion

• Support for robust implementation of existing IPRA statutes

Submit Your Public Comment: https://nmdoj.gov/get-help/inspection-of-public-records-act/

Whether you’ve personally struggled to access public records, witnessed government obstruction, or simply believe transparency is essential to democracy, your voice matters. The task force meetings are where policy direction gets set and where the balance between government convenience and public accountability is negotiated.

“Do not assume someone else will speak up,” accountability advocates emphasize. “These comment periods are where ordinary citizens can directly influence whether IPRA remains a tool for transparency or becomes another mechanism for government control.”

item.title: Timberon Water District in Freefall: Two Board Resignations, a Records Office in Turmoil, and a Community That’s Had Enough
item.description:
TIMBERON, N.M. — In the span of six weeks, the Timberon Water and Sanitation District has lost its board chairman, its vice chair, and — in a departure the district itself called sudden — the records custodian whose combative handling of public-records requests had already become a story of its own. Board Chairman Otis Price announced his resignation effective August 1, 2026. Vice Chair Caleb Flora resigned June 17. And records custodian Leo McAtee, who weeks earlier had told a reporter requesting public documents that he had “other work to do than play street lawyer” and stood by his description of a routine records request as a “scheme,” left the district so abruptly that General Manager Wendy Case spent, in her words, “the bigger part of the day” trying to determine which public-records requests remained unanswered.

Individually, any one of these departures might be unremarkable turnover at a small rural utility. Together, arriving as the district faces its most sustained public scrutiny in years, they read as something closer to an institution buckling under pressure it has spent months failing to relieve.

Three Departures, One Pattern

The district announced Price’s resignation through board secretary Nanette Cameron Thorell on the community’s Facebook page — a channel the district’s own board secretary has acknowledged rarely carries TWSD announcements at all. The notice was terse: Price was stepping down effective August 1, the board had roughly 30 days to appoint a replacement, and residents interested in “giving back to Timberon” were invited to apply. It was a near carbon copy, down to the wording, of the notice posted six weeks earlier announcing Flora’s departure.

McAtee’s exit followed a different, more contentious arc. In the week before he left, he was the subject of direct, on-the-record reporting over his handling of a records request tied to the district’s golf course lease and its ongoing boil-water advisories — a request he initially extended under the state’s “excessively burdensome” provision, then followed with correspondence that abandoned the language of records law almost entirely. He told the requesting reporter he saw “no requirement to trickle you out bits and parts of data,” suggested the reporter “should have been a responsible adult” and filed the request in smaller pieces, and reaffirmed that he considered “scheme” the most accurate word for what had been asked of him. Weeks later, Case’s email to the same reporter explaining McAtee’s departure noted staff were still trying to reconstruct which of his open requests had been answered and which hadn’t — meaning the hostility documented in his final weeks on the job outlasted his tenure, in the form of an unresolved backlog someone else now has to sort out.

A Board Already Running Thin

The math is not abstract. With both the chairman and vice chair seats vacant simultaneously, TWSD is operating on a reduced board at the exact moment New Mexico law puts a clock on how long that can continue. Under NMSA 1978 §73-21-13, a water and sanitation district board vacancy left unfilled after 30 days causes the district court with jurisdiction — Otero County District Court — to fill the seat itself. Two vacancies inside six weeks leaves the district with limited room before that deadline starts converting board appointments into court appointments.

Applicants for Price’s seat must be taxpaying electors residing within TWSD’s boundaries, with letters of interest due to the district office or by email to the board secretary by August 6. The remaining board is expected to fill the seat by majority vote at a public meeting — assuming it can convene a quorum willing to do the work, something recent meeting minutes suggest has not always been guaranteed.

A Community Past the Point of Patience

The public reaction to Price’s resignation notice, posted to the community Facebook page, was not sympathetic. Beneath the district’s formal announcement, community members responded with open sarcasm about the appointment process itself — mocking commentary questioning whether any appointment would meaningfully change how the district is run, and openly skeptical references to informal community factions perceived as controlling board decisions. This outlet is not republishing the specific names or labels used in those comments, since they amount to unverified, personal characterizations of private residents rather than reported fact — but the tenor of the response is itself notable: a community that has stopped treating board turnover as routine news and started treating it as further evidence of dysfunction.

That reaction doesn’t come from nowhere. It lands after a summer in which TWSD issued three precautionary boil-water advisories in five weeks; after the New Mexico Environment Department found the district failed to notify its own customers of a drinking-water violation for at least three months; after board records showed a 10-year lease of the district-owned golf course to a private operator for $1 a month, with no appraisal or competitive bid on record; after the community pool was shut for the season for lack of funds; and after the board began moving toward foreclosure on more than 200 delinquent ratepayer accounts even as its own infrastructure plan concedes the water system itself needs to be rebuilt. A state Public Regulation Commissioner has already floated stripping the board of control entirely through receivership — not a new idea for this district, which was placed under a court-ordered receivership once before, around 2008.

Pressure From Every Direction

What distinguishes this moment from earlier rough patches in TWSD’s history is the number of fronts converging on the board at once. The PRC has an open billing-audit docket it says the district still hasn’t proven it completed. A separate PRC complaint questions the legality of the district’s core non-water revenue source. The state Department of Justice found the board repeatedly violated the Open Meetings Act, with compliance deadlines that have now passed without documented proof of completion. NMED has the district on its public enforcement watch list. And an independent local news outlet has spent weeks publishing detailed, document-backed reporting on the golf course lease, the hidden violation, and the district’s own records office — reporting that, by its own account, prompted the burdensome-request fight with McAtee in the first place.

Board members resigning under that kind of sustained, simultaneous pressure — regulatory, legal, financial, and now openly public — is not something this article can attribute to any single cause, and neither Price, Flora, nor McAtee has publicly stated a reason for leaving beyond the brief notices the district itself posted. But the confluence is hard to ignore: a board losing members and a records office losing its custodian at precisely the moment the district’s failures have become the subject of sustained outside documentation, rather than something residents were left to describe secondhand.

What Comes Next

The immediate question is procedural: can a board now missing two of its usual leadership seats find replacements before the statutory clock hands that decision to a judge. The larger question is whether new appointees — chosen, per the district’s own posted criteria, from whichever residents step forward — can do anything the outgoing board could not: produce a credible infrastructure repair timeline, answer direct questions about tank levels and advisory status without deflecting to bulk records dumps, and rebuild a level of public trust that, on the evidence of this summer alone, has substantially eroded.

Note: This article draws on TWSD’s public notices, correspondence reviewed in connection with ongoing coverage of the district, and prior reporting on the district’s regulatory and governance matters. It does not attribute any individual’s resignation to a specific cause beyond what has been publicly stated, and it does not repeat unverified personal characterizations of private individuals made in public comments. It is a factual summary as a part of our ongoing investigative series.

item.title: In Memory of David Otto Bellows
item.description:
In Loving Memory of David Otto Bellows.

With heavy hearts, we announce the peaceful passing of David Otto Bellows on July 16, 2026. A devoted husband, loving father, and proud grandfather and great grandfather, Dave leaves behind a legacy of love, integrity, and strength.

Born in Alamogordo to Forest Otto Bellows and Ola Inez Galyeon, Dave grew up with a strong work ethic and an unshakable sense of responsibility. He dedicated many years to local construction businesses, building not only homes and structures but also a reputation for honesty, craftsmanship, and dedication. In his forties and through his retirement, he served in the Structure Shop for the 49th Civil Engineering at Holloman Air Force Base. His hands were calloused from labor, yet they were always gentle when holding his grandchildren and great grandchildren or helping family or neighbors in need.

Dave found the love of his life, Helen Bain, and they married on November 13, 2002. He quickly learned how busy life would be. Together, they built their home with their own hands... of it was done by them except the electrical. He was so proud of the home that they had created together.

Dave believed in the dignity of hard work and the value of keeping one’s word. He took immense pride in every beam he set and every foundation he poured, knowing his work would stand for generations. Outside of work, he found joy in fishing at Caballo, tending his garden, hunting, Nascar Racing, ol’ blue...his GMC truck, and cheering for the Dallas Cowboys. Above all else, he cherished time spent with his beloved family.

Dave is survived by his wife of almost twenty-four years, Helen Bellows. He is also survived by his children, Melissa Reynolds and Eric Rutherford of Alamogordo, and Bobby Bellows of Lubbock, TX. Dave leaves behind twelve grandchildren and five great grandchildren. He is survived by his brother, Bill Bellows of Wyoming; two of his sisters, Mickey Sidwell of Alabama and Rennie Parshall of Kansas; as well as numerous nieces and nephews who will forever carry his lessons, laughter, and love in their hearts.

He was preceded in death by his parents; his brothers, Gorman and Pat Bellows; sisters, Loretta Parks and Doris Davis. We know that Chloe, his dog, was awaiting him on the other side.

A celebration of Dave’s life will be held by close family and friends at a later date to share stories and honor the man who built so much more than buildings, he built a profound legacy of love, integrity, and strength.

Rest easy, Papa. Your work here is done, but your foundation will never crumble.

In lieu of flowers the family asks that you make a donation to the American Cancer Society. You may also visit findagrave.com to leave a flower.

item.title: Otero Arts presents Sue Nichols’ “The Light of La Luz” at Artspace August 2026
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO — Otero Arts will open “The Light of La Luz,” an exhibition of paintings and stained glass by New Mexico artist Sue Nichols, with a reception from 5 to 7 p.m. Friday, August 7, at Otero Artspace, 1118 Indiana Avenue at 12th Street.

The show gathers 33 works in oil, watercolor, and stained glass drawn from a career spent looking closely at one corner of the world. Nichols did not come to the land by birth. Born in Carlsbad and raised in Alamogordo, she was a young woman working at the Ruidoso Downs racetrack when she married her high school sweetheart and moved to his family’s orchard ranch in the Sacramento Mountains near La Luz. She has remained there ever since, and for decades that ground has been her central subject.

The exhibition ranges widely while holding to a single sensibility. Paintings of the working land—among them “Way of Life” and the oil painting “Hell or High Water”—share the room with wildlife studies such as “Late Summer Meadows,” quiet still lifes drawn from her own rooms and gardens, and figurative pieces that catch ordinary people in unguarded moments. Also on view are works in stained glass, the discipline Nichols has practiced for decades through her studio, Canyon Glassworks, including the three-panel Spirit Dancers screen and the Peace panel.

“I try not to be too specific in the narrative, so the viewer can complete the story and have their own relationship with the work,” Nichols says. “Much of the world I paint is quietly vanishing. My hope is to preserve a little of its beauty and its history, and to help someone feel it the way I do.”

Nichols earned her Bachelor of Fine Arts at New Mexico State University. She has completed more than 70 commissioned stained-glass works and is a trusted source for stained-glass restoration throughout southern New Mexico. Her work is held in private collections and shown in galleries across the state.

Otero Artspace is open Thursday through Sunday from 1 to 4 p.m. The exhibition continues through Saturday, August 29.

The show is supported by NM Arts, the Department of Cultural Affairs, and the National Endowment for the Arts. For more information, visit oteroarts.org.

item.title: Timberon Water Board Loses Three Leaders in Six Weeks as Scrutiny of the District Intensifies
item.description:
TIMBERON, N.M. — In the span of roughly six weeks, the Timberon Water and Sanitation District has lost three people from its leadership: a vice chairman who resigned, a board chairman who has announced his resignation effective August 1, and the district’s longtime records custodian, Leo McAtee, who is no longer employed by TWSD. The district has not stated why McAtee left.

The departures land in the middle of the heaviest outside scrutiny TWSD has faced in years — state enforcement findings, a boil-water advisory, a $1-a-month golf-course lease, and a series of records requests this outlet has pursued since early July.

The timeline

• Six weeks ago (mid-June): TWSD Vice Chairman Caleb Flora resigned from the board.

• July 13, 2026: In response to this outlet’s IPRA request for water-testing records, McAtee wrote that he had determined the request “excessively burdensome and broad,” said he could not produce records incrementally, and described this outlet’s characterization of the process as an objection rather than, in his words, “reality.” He separately stood by an earlier description of the request as a “scheme.”

• July 16, 2026: In a markedly different, more cooperative email three days later, McAtee sent a partial response to the same IPRA request along with a cost schedule, explained his preference for no-cost digital delivery over paper, and — regarding a separate, larger records request for insurance data tied to the district’s High Country Lounge — committed to having “all ready to send back with reply on or before July 23, 2026 by COB.”

• July 23, 2026: The date McAtee committed to in writing passed without the promised production.

• July 2026, after July 23: McAtee left TWSD. In a July 24 email to this outlet, TWSD staffer Wendy Case wrote that McAtee “left suddenly” and that the office was still working to reconstruct which of this outlet’s records requests had been received and answered, having so far located three. Whether McAtee’s departure was voluntary has not been confirmed; a request for comment on the circumstances is pending with the district.

• Late July: Board Chairman Otis Price announced his resignation, effective August 1.

It’s worth noting the record on McAtee is not one-note: the July 13 email was combative, but the July 16 email was detailed, professional, and included a specific delivery commitment. What’s notable is not that he was uniformly obstructive, but that a specific, self-imposed deadline — one he set, not one imposed on him — went unmet before he left the district’s employment entirely.

The documented basis for the scrutiny

None of this happened in a vacuum. Over the past several months, this outlet has published a sustained record of reporting on TWSD, including:

• “Timberon Water and Sanitation District Grapples with Chronic Violations, Soaring Rates, and Questions of Oversight and Accountability” (May 2, 2026) — documenting regulatory lapses, high water-loss rates, and a pending PRC complaint (Case 25-00011-UT) raising the possibility of receivership.

• “Boiling Water, Empty Taps, and an Unreported Violation — While Timberon’s Water District Gave Away Its Golf Course for $1 a Month” (mid-July 2026) — reporting a June 9, 2026 NMED Notice of Violation finding TWSD failed to notify customers of an earlier drinking-water violation, alongside the district’s 10-year, $1-a-month lease of its golf course.

• “Timberon’s Water Crisis: A Clean Sample, a Month Without Reliable Service, and a Hidden Violation” (July 11, 2026) — covering a month of low-pressure and boil-water conditions on Tank #2 and the certified sample results that followed.

• “Pump Was No Surprise: Timberon Water Board’s Emergency Meeting Draws Scrutiny” (July 18, 2026) — questioning whether a same-day “emergency” meeting to address a pump problem the board had already discussed for six days complied with the Open Meetings Act. (Direct link not confirmed at time of writing; available via this outlet’s Timberon coverage archive.)

• Multiple public-interest IPRA requests filed with TWSD beginning in early July 2026, seeking water testing records, sample logs, correspondence with NMED, and insurance records tied to the district-leased High Country Lounge.

McAtee’s written responses to these requests were mixed: an initial reply characterized the request as “excessively burdensome and broad” and, separately, as a “scheme,” while a follow-up days later was cooperative and detailed, including a specific — and ultimately unmet — commitment to deliver outstanding records by July 23, 2026.

Not the only investigation

This outlet’s coverage is not the sole source of outside pressure on TWSD, and it would be inaccurate to suggest otherwise. State regulators and other independent news organizations have been examining the district’s problems for months, in some cases well before this outlet’s most recent reporting:

• New Mexico Public Regulation Commission: At a November 2025 PRC hearing on a separate complaint against TWSD, Commissioner Patrick O’Connell publicly floated placing the district into receivership — a step that would strip the elected board of control entirely — asking, “How many more Timberon issues do we need to see before we put the pieces together and say, ‘We need a bigger solution than a fine?’” A prior TWSD board chair, David Cruey, told Source New Mexico the district needs $45–50 million for a full infrastructure overhaul rather than a state takeover. (Source NM, Dec. 4, 2025)

• New Mexico Environment Department: NMED’s Water Protection Compliance & Enforcement Bureau issued TWSD a Notice of Violation on June 9, 2026, finding the district had failed to notify its own customers of an earlier drinking-water violation issued three months prior, and failed to certify that notification to the state.

Recent independent sourcing: 

As recently as January 2026, Source New Mexico — a nonprofit statehouse newsroom unaffiliated with this outlet — reported that the PRC’s push for state intervention in a separate small utility “follows a similar request seeking state intervention in Timberon in September,” and noted Timberon’s system loses as much as 85% of its water to leaky pipes. (Source NM, Jan. 13, 2026) A February 2026 Source NM piece on a different troubled utility again cited Timberon’s water-loss rate as a point of comparison for the scale of the state’s rural water crisis. (Source NM, Feb. 26, 2026)

The upshot: 

TWSD’s problems were on the state’s radar, and in the pages of an independent statehouse newsroom, well before this outlet’s most recent round of coverage. Whatever role this outlet’s reporting has played, it is one strand of scrutiny among several, running alongside — not ahead of — regulators’ own findings.

A Facebook page, and a question of focus

Separately, in recent days, a Facebook page created last week posted a series of items examining the corporate and nonprofit structure behind this outlet, its ownership, and this reporter’s personal history.

Whether that page is connected to anyone at TWSD as speculated by locals in Timberon and whether its posts amount to an attempt at retaliation for the scrutiny the district is under, cannot be confirmed as of yet, and this outlet does not assert either as fact.

What can be said is this: those posts have not, at any point, addressed the substance of what residents are actually owed — a functioning water system, a credible plan to fix it, and an honest accounting of the district’s finances.

Rather than engage the transparency questions, propose a plan to repair the system’s chronic losses, or work toward public consensus on a fix, the response — from whoever is behind it — has been to redirect the conversation toward the ownership structure of a media company. That may or may not be coincidental. It is, at minimum, notable: it is not an answer to any of the questions TWSD’s ratepayers are actually asking and looks to most as a pitiful look of desperation by a bitter former employee and TWSD insiders. 

What we can and can’t say

It is a fair, documented fact that three leadership departures have occurred during the same window as this outlet’s most intensive coverage of the district. It is not something this outlet can currently prove — and does not claim — that the coverage caused any of the three departures.

TWSD has not offered a public explanation connecting the departures to press scrutiny, litigation exposure, the pending PRC matter, or anything else, and no such connection should be assumed absent that explanation.

This outlet has asked TWSD directly whether McAtee’s departure was voluntary and who has taken over as records custodian. That request, along with a formal notice regarding a since-expired IPRA response deadline, is pending as of publication. This story will be updated with the district’s response other then the one seeking clarification that 3 IPRA’s are open and pending. 

This article reflects a series of articles and information as well as this outlet’s own prior reporting as of July 26, 2026, and will be updated as TWSD responds to pending requests for comment.

item.title: In Memory of Preston Varner Stevens
item.description:
Preston Varner Stevens, passed away on July 23, 2026, in Las Cruces, New Mexico, surrounded by his family after a lengthy illness. He was born in Childress, Texas, and lived his years with faith, dignity, and a steadfast commitment to serving others.

Preston was a Christian man whose life reflected the values he held dear. He believed in hard work, integrity, and the importance of walking faithfully with the Lord through every season of life. Those who knew him will remember his steady presence, his kind spirit, and the quiet strength with which he met both the ordinary and the difficult moments of life. He was a man who carried himself with humility and grace, and he left a lasting impression on all who were blessed to know him.

He proudly served his country and then received his Bachelor of Business Administration from West Texas State University in Canyon, Texas, and later earned his Juris Doctor degree from Texas Tech Law School. His education laid the foundation for a distinguished legal career and a lifetime of public service. Preston was admitted to the State Bar of Texas and served as County Attorney for Wheeler County, Texas. He later retired after 25 years of service as First Assistant District Attorney in Odessa, Texas, where he earned the respect of colleagues and the gratitude of the community he served so faithfully. His dedication to justice and public service was recognized when January 8, 2004, was proclaimed Preston Stevens’ Day in Odessa, Texas, a fitting tribute to a career marked by honor and perseverance.

After retirement, Preston and his wife moved to the mountains near Cloudcroft, New Mexico, where he found peace in the beauty of God’s creation and the slower rhythm of mountain life. He served as President of the Robin Hood Water Users’ Association and gave his time as Sunday School Director for Mayhill Baptist Church. His faith was not merely spoken but lived, and he served his church and community with a willing heart. He found joy in simple pleasures, including travel, fly fishing, reading, and watching westerns, and these interests brought him comfort and enjoyment throughout his life.

Preston cherished his family. His wife, children, grandchildren, and great grandchildren were a continuous source of happiness and the most special and treasured relationships in his life. He is survived by his wife, Valerie Stevens; his son, James Stevens; his daughter, Jennifer Spaulding and her husband, Brandon; his grandsons, Connor Stevens and his wife, Katy, Brex Stevens, and Ryan Spaulding; his granddaughter, Emily Markos and her husband, Alex; his sister, Nonie Cawthon; and numerous nieces, nephews, great-nieces, and great-nephews.

Preston’s life was a testimony to the truth of Proverbs 22:1, which says, “A good name is to be chosen rather than great riches, and favor is better than silver or gold.” Though his passing brings sorrow, those who love him take comfort in knowing that he is now at peace in the presence of his Savior. His earthly journey has ended, but the legacy of his faith, devotion, and love will continue to bless his family and all who knew him.

He will be deeply missed and lovingly remembered. May the Lord comfort all who mourn his passing and grant peace to those who loved him.

Preston was a 32° Scottish Rite Mason, the family requests that in lieu of flowers donations be made to Scottish Rite for Children Hospital in Dallas, TX.

The funeral service for Preston Stevens will be held at 10:00 am Monday July 27, 2026 at Mayhill Baptist Church in Mayhill, New Mexico. Burial will be at Childress Cemetery in Childress, Texas Tuesday the 28th at 10:00 am.

item.title: At Tularosa Vigil, Cordova Announces She Will Address UN General Assembly — First Time Alamogordo, Tularosa, Carrizozo and Otero County Will Be Named There Together
item.description:
By Chris Edwards | Alamogordo Town News

TULAROSA, N.M. — Under a sky that opened into a downpour and then, just as suddenly, a double rainbow, several  people from the broader community gathered Saturday evening at Tularosa Veterans Memorial Park for the Tularosa Basin Downwinders Consortium’s annual candlelight vigil honoring the more than 900 known victims of radiation sickness tied to the 1945 Trinity nuclear test.

It was at that vigil that TBDC co-founder Tina Cordova announced she has been invited to address the United Nations General Assembly — a moment she told this outlet will mark the first time the communities of Alamogordo, Tularosa, Carrizozo, and Otero County as a whole will be named together before the UN body. Cordova confirmed the appearance directly to this outlet following the event.

A night of remembrance

The vigil began at 7:30 p.m. and continued into the evening. For each of the more than 900 names remembered, organizers lit a luminary, tolled a bell, read the name aloud, and struck a drumbeat — a ceremony repeated hundreds of times over the course of the night for people from Alamogordo, Tularosa, Carrizozo, and across Otero County who died of illnesses tied to radiation exposure from the Trinity blast.

Attendees included representatives from the offices of U.S. Rep. Gabe Vasquez and U.S. Sen. Ben Ray Luján, along with Alamogordo Mayor Sharon McDonald, Tularosa Mayor Deborah Cooksey, and Alamogordo City Commissioner Warren Robinson.

The UN announcement

Cordova’s forthcoming UN General Assembly address adds an international dimension to a fight she has waged for two decades. The Tularosa Basin Downwinders Consortium, which she co-founded in 2005, has long pressed for the federal government to acknowledge and compensate the New Mexicans exposed to fallout from the world’s first nuclear detonation — communities that, unlike downwinders in Nevada, Utah, and Idaho, were left out of the original 1990 Radiation Exposure Compensation Act (RECA) for decades.

The announcement comes amid an active push in Washington to expand that compensation further. Just days before the vigil, on July 14, Cordova joined U.S. Rep. Gabe Vasquez and members of Congress from Missouri and Nevada at a virtual news conference to back the Radiation Exposure Reauthorization Act of 2026, a bill that would extend RECA’s application deadline by 15 years, raise compensation from $100,000 to $150,000, expand the list of qualifying illnesses, and allow the use of affidavits for claimants unable to produce decades-old medical records. According to Department of Justice figures cited at that news conference, roughly 4,400 RECA claims have been filed since the 2025 expansion, with 558 approved and $55.8 million paid out so far.

“I think that it’s high time our government realizes that we are not going to stand for justice for some,” Cordova said at a July 14 news conference. “We are in favor of justice for not just a few, but justice for the many.”

What comes next

This outlet has not yet confirmed the specific date of Cordova’s UN General Assembly appearance or the session under which she will speak; that information is expected to follow. This story will be updated with those details, along with any additional confirmation from Cordova, the Tularosa Basin Downwinders Consortium, or United Nations sources, as they become available.

This article reflects information confirmed directly with Tina Cordova and this outlet’s on-the-ground reporting from the July 25, 2026 vigil, along with prior reporting on the Radiation Exposure Reauthorization Act of 2026.

Alamogordo Chamber of Commerce Executive Director Adam Hoppes will then brief commissioners on the Chamber's activities over the past year, including the completed second phase of the Gateway Freedom Monument at the U.S. 70/U.S. 54 interchange and the Chamber's pursuit of AETC's Altus Trophy for community support.

Consent Agenda

Eight items are slated for the consent agenda, where they will be voted on as a single block unless a commissioner asks to pull one for separate discussion. Among them:

Commissioners will consider approval of the Fiscal Year 2026 annual reports submitted by five city boards and committees — the Airport Advisory Board, the Airport Zoning Board, the Alamogordo Public Library Advisory Board, the Parks & Recreation Advisory Board, and the Senior Volunteer Programs Advisory Council — as required under Section 2-04-050 of the city code. Separate articles examining each report appear alongside this one.

An agreement with Otero County would bring the Alamogordo Public Library a $35,000 reimbursable grant to extend library collections to county residents outside city limits, helping the library meet a required cash match with the State Library.

A second Otero County agreement covers Alamo Senior Center services for county residents, budgeted at $52,305 — $30,789 for home-delivered meals and $21,516 for transportation.

Commissioners will also consider Change Order No. 3 on the Great Blocks MainStreet project, adding $34,188.11 to the contract with Crosstown Construction & Trucking, LLC. The change order covers irrigation and electrical cost increases, an unforeseen trench-drain relocation, overhead structure modifications, additional asphalt and striping work on 8th and 10th streets and New York Avenue, and conduit repair. City staff say roughly $20,000 of the added cost is expected to be recouped from the project's structural engineer under an errors-and-omissions claim. The change order would bring the total contract value to $3,338,728.56, up from an original $2,564,473.78.

A contract award to Zia Therapy Center, Inc., doing business as Ztrans, would formalize fixed-route and paratransit transportation services for the city under RFP 2026-004, at a cost of $259,968.30 — an amount already approved as part of the FY27 budget. The company was the sole respondent to the RFP, released May 31 and due July 1.

Commissioner Hernandez currently represents the city on the SNMEDD/COG board. This item requires a roll call vote as a resolution.

Unfinished Business

Commissioners return to Ordinance 1724, which would repeal Chapter 22 of the city code governing subdivision requirements and replace it with updated subdivision regulations under a new Chapter 20, Land Development Code. The commission tabled the ordinance at its June 9 meeting to give staff and commissioners more time to review the rewrite. Tuesday's vote on final adoption and publication requires a roll call.

item.title: Airport Advisory Board's FY26 Report Shows Runway Rehab Costs Climbing Toward $50 Million as Board Pushes Grant Strategy
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO, N.M. — July 27, 2026 —

Of the five city boards and committees submitting Fiscal Year 2026 annual reports for commission approval Tuesday, the Airport Advisory Board's is by far the most active, documenting a full slate of monthly meetings from July 2025 through June 2026 under Chairman Manuel Gonzales Jr.

The board, created under city code section 4-02-040 to advise the city commission on airport construction, facilities and operating policy, met the first Thursday of nearly every month during the reporting period. Its five current members — Gonzales, Vice Chairman Lance Grace, Erich Wuersching, Mark Werner and Robert Hicks — posted strong attendance across all twelve scheduled meetings, with a handful of individual absences. The board is advised by Airport Manager Troy Orr and liaison Kris Salas, the Community Services Department's executive assistant.

Runway rehabilitation costs rising

The board's central preoccupation through the year was the Runway 4/22 rehabilitation project. Early in the reporting period, consultant Delta Consultants was working toward a draft Preliminary Engineering Report, and by August 2025 the board was already pushing to have the airport's classification upgraded to C3 to secure future federal funding. By February 2026, the estimated project cost had grown to roughly $8 million, which the board attributed to five years of rising material costs. By April 2026, with the FAA's Fort Worth office reviewing 20-year design options within the PER, projected costs for a comprehensive rehabilitation had expanded further, into a range city aviation officials described as the mid-twenties to $50 million — though those officials also told the board they supported completing the work in a single phase rather than piecemeal. In May 2026, the board directed Delta to submit the FAA's final design grant application by a June 1 deadline in pursuit of C2 runway standards.

In December 2025, the board also authorized a request for proposals for an updated air service market study to support travel needs tied to Holloman Air Force Base and to pursue Part 139 certification for the airport, and continued refining that study's scope through the spring after board members flagged wide-ranging vendor quotes. Delta Consultants was announced in February 2026 as the airport's selected firm for a new four-year consulting contract.

Fees and lease terms revised

The board approved several financial changes during the year. In March 2026, it documented a Consumer Price Index-based increase in the airport's ground lease rate, from 15.4 cents to 15.8 cents per square foot, while leaving Aero Club monthly parking rates unchanged. In May 2026, the board formalized an increase in commercial air-tanker landing fees, from 30 cents to 40 cents per 1,000 pounds. Members also spent much of the fall and winter reworking standard lease and "minimum standards" language covering flight instruction and flying clubs, ultimately agreeing that a flying-club framework was the best way to preserve non-commercial flight instruction without imposing commercial brick-and-mortar requirements on part-time instructors. In November 2025, the board removed a disputed insurance clause on hangar damage from the boilerplate lease, replacing it with defined rebuild-or-clear-the-site options for lessees; by February 2026 it had also tightened the damage threshold that triggers those provisions to require damage exceeding 50% of a hangar's insured value.

Monument, infrastructure and other business

The board tracked the F-4 Gateway Freedom Monument through to completion, following its December 8, 2025, ribbon-cutting and a Holloman Air Force Base flyover, with mechanical and paint work confirmed complete earlier in the fall. In June 2026, District 5 Commissioner Al Hernandez appeared before the board to discuss public criticism of city infrastructure spending, and the board highlighted the airport access road as a potential candidate for outside grant funding. That same month, the board rolled a separate $109,000 state grant for an electrical vault design into the broader runway project to create what members called a single "shovel-ready" package, and it affirmed November 7, 2026, as the date for its next open house.

Other actions during the year included accepting a no-cost offer from the Alamogordo Chamber of Commerce to use an automated grant-search tool, applying for a decommissioned Air Force T-38 aircraft for static display, formally recommending that anyone at the airport call 911 in a safety emergency, and repairing perimeter fencing cut by trespassers.

The board meets the first Thursday of each month; its regular July meeting was rescheduled to July 9 this year to accommodate the Independence Day holiday and the second phase of the F-4 Monument dedication.

item.title: Library Advisory Board Cites Lingering COVID Fallout, Road Construction in FY26 Annual Report
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO, N.M. — July 27, 2026 —

The Alamogordo Public Library Advisory Board's annual report for the year ending June 30, 2026, one of five board and committee reports before the city commission for approval Tuesday, describes a board that met regularly but irregularly — convening eight times out of twelve possible months — while grappling with what members describe as a persistent, multi-year decline in library visits.

The board, created under Article 16-02 of the city code, advises both the city and Otero County commissions on library management and is tasked with keeping itself informed of library needs, recommending facility and program development, and encouraging greater public use of the library. It is composed of seven unpaid members serving two-year terms: five city residents appointed by the mayor and two county residents outside city limits appointed by the Otero County Commission. Kim Underwood, the city librarian, serves as an ex officio member.

According to the report, the board did not meet in January or February 2026 due to illness, nor in April; a called meeting in May failed to reach a quorum. Aside from those lapses, the report describes attendance over the year as "very good," with absences attributable to illness or excused reasons. The board's current roster includes Vice Chair Rhonda Alterson, Cynthia Stevenson, Chairperson Richard Warren — now in his fourth term — John Davis, Pamela Vesey, county appointee Brad Nichols, and one vacant county seat.

The report attributes the ongoing softness in library usage to a combination of factors: continuing fallout from the COVID-19 pandemic, road construction around the library at 920 Oregon Avenue, and a shrinking school-age population that has reduced the number of student visitors. Board discussions during the year centered on whether current marketing efforts are adequately building public awareness of library programs and services, with members exploring additional outreach strategies. Warren, an American Library Association member, is credited in the report with relaying security updates and training opportunities to fellow board members, and with helping review both ongoing and new library programming, including discussion of potential expanded hours.

The report was submitted by Warren on June 24, 2026, with Underwood and liaison Melissa Garcia credited for maintaining member packets and years of meeting minutes for easy reference. The board meets at 4 p.m. on the second Wednesday of the month, in person or remotely.

item.title: Alamogordo Parks and Recreation Advisory Board Reports Busy Year of Improvements and Strategic Planning
item.description:
The Alamogordo Parks and Recreation Advisory Board has released its annual report for fiscal year 2026, highlighting a productive year marked by governance improvements, major infrastructure initiatives, and increased collaboration with city agencies and schools.

Covering the period from July 1, 2025, through June 30, 2026, the board’s report details significant progress on multiple fronts, including the development of new training standards, oversight of the Alameda Park Zoo transition, and continued monitoring of the planned natatorium facility.

Strengthening Governance and Leadership

The seven-member board, comprised of five members appointed by the Mayor with City Commission approval and two members selected by the Alamogordo Public Schools Board of Education, focused on internal governance improvements this fiscal year.

In July 2025, the board approved updated bylaws to ensure compliance with city ordinances governing member removal and term limits. Later, in April 2026, members adopted a further amendment requiring periodic review of bylaws every three years, with the next comprehensive review scheduled for 2028.

“These changes demonstrate our commitment to maintaining strong governance practices and operational clarity,” the board indicated in its report.

New Training Program Launched

Recognizing the importance of board member education, the Parks and Recreation Advisory Board initiated development of a comprehensive training program designed to prepare members for their advisory responsibilities.

The training plan includes modules on the Open Meetings Act (OMA), ethics, roles and responsibilities, and Robert’s Rules of Order. To support new members, the board established an “onboarding buddy” mentor system pairing experienced board members with newcomers to facilitate a smoother transition into their advisory roles.

Major Projects Under Way

The board continued active oversight of several significant city projects during the reporting period.

Natatorium Project Advances

The new aquatic center, a long-awaited addition to Alamogordo’s recreational infrastructure, received focused attention from board members. The board provided critical input on facility design and recommended a Sprung Structure for the new natatorium. Members participated in community naming surveys and regularly monitored funding status and bond progress throughout the year.

Zoo Integration Complete

In a major transition, the Alameda Park Zoo was officially transferred to the Parks & Recreation Department on November 1, 2025. The board closely monitored this integration process to ensure a smooth transition and continued quality of the facility’s operations.

Ongoing Maintenance and Facilities

The board tracked progress on several other key initiatives, including work on the Dudley School Playground renovation, warranty repairs for playground shade structures, and ongoing maintenance of pickleball courts. The board also noted participation in the Goat Grazing Green Initiative trial program, which explores sustainable landscaping solutions.

Strategic Planning and Community Coordination

Looking beyond the current fiscal year, board members advocated for active participation in the upcoming City Comprehensive Plan update. They also discussed strategies to better align board input with the city’s December-July budgeting cycle, aiming to improve coordination between park and recreation planning and the city’s financial planning process.

Board members emphasized the importance of continued coordination with the Alamogordo Public Schools and other governmental agencies to ensure parks and recreation services meet community needs comprehensively.

Meeting Attendance

During the fiscal year, the board held three quarterly meetings—in October 2025, January 2026, and April 2026. The board typically meets quarterly and continues to welcome community input on parks and recreation matters.

Looking Forward

The Parks and Recreation Advisory Board report underscores the city’s commitment to maintaining and improving recreational infrastructure while fostering community engagement. As Alamogordo continues to grow, the board’s role in advising on policies, fee structures, and development standards becomes increasingly important to the city’s quality of life.

The board’s dual focus on operational excellence and strategic planning positions Alamogordo’s parks and recreation services to serve residents effectively for years to come.

The full annual report from the Alamogordo Parks and Recreation Advisory Board for Fiscal Year 2026 will be presented to the City Commission on July 28, 2026, as part of the city’s regular reporting requirements for all city boards and committees.

item.title: Mayor McDonald’s Vision May Come to Life: Alamogordo May Launch First-Ever Youth Commission
item.description:
For the first time in Alamogordo’s history, high school students may have a formal seat at the table where city decisions are made. The Mayor’s Youth Advisory Commission (MYAC), if approved by the City Commission on July 28, represents a bold new vision for civic engagement from Mayor Sharon McDonald—one that recognizes young people not as the future, but as essential voices for today.

“Step up. Speak out. Help shape Alamogordo’s future,” the program’s motto says. It’s an invitation that reflects McDonald’s conviction that meaningful change requires hearing from all generations, especially those who will live with the decisions made today for decades to come.

A Mayor’s Mission to Hear Youth Voices

Mayor McDonald has made youth engagement a centerpiece of her leadership. The MYAC represents the culmination of months of planning and reflects her belief that local government must actively seek out the perspectives, energy, and idealism that young people bring to community problem-solving.

“This is not just another program,” McDonald said in promoting the initiative. “This is about recognizing that our teenagers have valuable insights about what matters to them and to our community. When we listen to youth, we make better decisions.”

The MYAC is designed with genuine power-sharing in mind. These won’t be student representatives sitting silently in the back of city chambers. Instead, 16 youth commissioners—selected from Alamogordo high schools and NMSU-A—will hold elected leadership positions, run their own meetings, manage their own budget, and directly advise the Mayor on issues affecting their generation and the broader community.

Breaking New Ground

Alamogordo joins a growing national movement of cities that are investing in youth civic participation. But for this community, the MYAC represents uncharted territory. No previous mayor or commission has created such a formal, structured platform for youth voice in municipal governance.

“What makes this groundbreaking is not just that we’re inviting young people to participate,”… “It’s that we’re giving them real responsibility, real leadership, and real authority to shape priorities and drive projects,” explained Shelley Dowhanik-Baron, Community Development Director for the City of Alamogordo along with Co-Chair Vesta Sherrie Edmonds as the citizen advocate leader who led the initiative’s development phased 

The commission will consist of:

• 3 commissioners each from grades 8, 9, 10, 11, and 12

• 1 representative from NMSU-A

• Youth-elected officers including Chair, Vice-Chair, Secretary, Treasurer, and Media Coordinator

• Monthly meetings run by the students themselves, following Robert’s Rules of Order

Listening to the Next Generation

McDonald’s commitment to hearing from youth comes at a critical time. Across the country, young people are increasingly vocal about issues affecting them—mental health, climate change, education quality, economic opportunity, social justice, and their role in shaping their communities. The MYAC provides a structured channel for Alamogordo’s teenagers to voice these concerns directly to city leadership.

“Young people have ideas,” McDonald emphasized. “They understand technology, social media, and modern communication in ways we don’t. They have perspectives on public safety, recreation, economic development, and environmental issues that can genuinely improve how we govern.”

The program’s design reflects this philosophy. Rather than asking youth to simply advise on pre-determined issues, MYAC commissioners will identify their own priorities and propose projects aligned with their concerns.

Building Civic Leaders Today

Beyond the immediate community service and advisory functions, the MYAC serves a larger purpose: building a generation of engaged citizens. By giving teenagers meaningful roles in local government now, Alamogordo is investing in future voters, volunteers, board members, and leaders.

Research shows that young people who participate in civic engagement at the high school level are significantly more likely to remain civically active throughout their lives. They’re more likely to vote, volunteer, and run for office as adults.

“We’re not just asking our young people to clean up parks and volunteer at food banks—though those are important,” McDonald noted. “We’re teaching them how local government works, how to lead meetings, manage budgets, and advocate for change. We’re preparing them to be the leaders Alamogordo needs in 2030, 2040, and beyond.”

What MYAC Will Do

The Mayor’s Youth Advisory Commission will operate through both direct service and advocacy:

Service Projects:

• Community clean-ups and beautification efforts

• Food, toy, and school supply drives

• Senior center and animal shelter support

• Youth forums on issues like bullying, mental health, and youth-police relations

• Support for local events and community organizations

Civic Engagement:

• Advisory input on municipal issues and planning (such as the upcoming Comprehensive Master Plan)

• “Careers in Local Government” day for younger students

• Tours of municipal facilities and offices

• Participation in City Commission meetings

• Youth Lobby Day at the State Capitol

Leadership Development:

• Workshops on government, financial literacy, public speaking, media literacy, and advocacy

• Guest speakers from city departments, nonprofits, businesses, and Holloman Air Force Base

• Mentorship from city staff and community leaders

• Real budget and project management experience

The Details

The MYAC will meet monthly on the second Monday from 4:45 to 6:00 p.m. at Dudley School Community Center. The program carries a modest first-year budget of $3,100 for marketing, recruitment, supplies, training, and meeting support.

Importantly, the city’s commitment extends beyond dollars. The City Commission has pledged to:

• Support broad recruitment of commissioners and mentors

• Encourage schools, businesses, and community organizations to participate

• Promote youth voice in municipal decisions

• Receive annual reports and presentations from commissioners

Applications will be accepted through August 24, 2026, at www.alamogordo.gov/MYAC.

Selected youth commissioners will be sworn in at the September 8 City Commission meeting, with the inaugural meeting scheduled for September 14.

There are no experience requirements. The program seeks to represent diverse youth voices, welcoming students interested in leadership, service, government, or any aspect of community life.

A Model for the Future?

McDonald’s vision for the MYAC extends beyond its immediate impact. City officials hope the program becomes a model for youth engagement that could be replicated in schools, nonprofits, and other organizations throughout Alamogordo and beyond.

“If this works—and we believe it will—we’re showing other communities that young people are ready and willing to help govern,” an external youth advocate said. “We’re not talking about youth advisory commissions as something we might do someday. This city is about doing it right now.”

The timing is deliberate. With Alamogordo facing important decisions about housing development, air service, economic growth, and quality of life, McDonald wanted youth perspectives at the table.

“These young people will inherit the decisions we’re making today about water security, trails, economic development, and community character,” the Mayor noted. “It only makes sense to have their voices heard in those decisions right now and how to expand services and better engage youth in the future.”

Why It Matters

The MYAC reflects a fundamental shift in how Alamogordo views its young residents. Rather than seeing them as passive recipients of adult decisions, the city is recognizing them as active stakeholders in their community’s future.

For students, the benefits are significant:

• Real leadership experience and elected responsibilities

• Hands-on learning about municipal government

• Community service hours for college applications and scholarships

• Direct access to city officials and decision-makers

• Mentorship and skill-building in communication, advocacy, and problem-solving

For Alamogordo, the benefits are equally important:

• Fresh perspectives on community challenges

• Increased youth participation in civic life

• Service projects addressing real community needs

• Stronger connection between city government and the next generation

• A pipeline of engaged citizens who understand and care about their community

Looking Forward

The MYAC launch represents just the beginning of Mayor McDonald’s effort to deepen youth engagement. Applications open August 12, with the deadline set for August 24. Recruitment materials are being distributed to schools, community centers, and online through the city’s website and social media.

For teenagers wondering if their voice matters, if city leaders actually want to hear from them, the MYAC sends a clear message: yes.

“This is for the young person who cares about their community but wasn’t sure how to get involved,” advocates suggest“This is for the student who has ideas about how to make Alamogordo better. This is for anyone in grades 8-12 who wants to learn, lead, and make a difference.”

The Commission selecting 16 youth commissioners will be Alamogordo’s newest civic leaders, answerable to the Mayor and the commission, accountable to their peers, and responsible for representing the voice of youth in city government.

It’s a responsibility they’ll now have the chance to accept.

The Mayor’s Youth Advisory Commission is a great idea!

item.title: Skaggs Must Remain Jailed As Legal Battle Intensifies Over High-Profile Death
item.description:
LAS CRUCES, N.M. — In a significant legal development for a case that has captivated southern New Mexico, the state Court of Appeals has upheld the pretrial detention of Kimberly Skaggs, the former treasurer of the Republican Party of New Mexico, keeping her behind bars as she awaits trial for the June death of cyclist Andrew Brown. Skaggs has deep ties to both Tularosa and Las Cruces shaking both communities. 

The decision, issued this week, represents a major setback for Skaggs’ legal defense team, which had aggressively challenged a district court’s June 29 ruling ordering her detention without bond. Her attorneys had argued the original detention order relied on procedural errors and failed to account for her previously clean criminal record and community ties.

But the appellate court’s affirmation of the detention order sends a clear message: in the eyes of New Mexico’s judicial system, the evidence against Skaggs—and the circumstances surrounding Brown’s death—paint a picture serious enough to justify keeping her locked up during the months or years of litigation ahead.

The Tragic Incident and Alleged Cover-Up

On the evening of June 22, Andrew Brown, 40, was riding his bicycle across North Fairacres Road just west of Las Cruces when he was struck by a black Cadillac Escalade allegedly operated by Skaggs at high speed. Brown suffered catastrophic injuries, including a compound leg fracture with bone protruding through the skin, and was pronounced dead at the scene.

What prosecutors characterize as consciousness of guilt followed: instead of remaining at the scene, Skaggs allegedly fled, attempted to hide the vehicle at another property she owned, and—most significantly—changed the vehicle’s license plate from one bearing a “U.S. Support Our Troops” message to a different plate.

“On the 22nd, this is the part that bothers me,” District Judge Conrad Perea said during the detention hearing. “A license plate that we already have come to learn was a ‘U.S. Support Our Troops License Plate’ was changed immediately, and became a new license plate.”

The appellate court’s affirmation was bolstered by details of Skaggs’ driving history. Court documents revealed she had appeared in New Mexico courts six times on speeding charges, and in 2025 received a warning for racing on streets and exhibition driving. In one incident that year, a police officer clocked her traveling 88 miles per hour in a 35 mile-per-hour zone. This pattern suggested to both prosecutors and the courts that reckless driving was not an anomaly but a behavioral thread in her history.

The Defense’s Argument and the Court’s Response

Skaggs’ legal team mounted an aggressive appeal, arguing the district court made procedural errors and that prosecutors failed to meet New Mexico’s stringent standards for pretrial detention. Under state law, prosecutors must prove both that a defendant poses a danger and that no reasonable release conditions—such as electronic monitoring or travel restrictions—could protect public safety. A 2023 New Mexico Supreme Court ruling further restricted detention by prohibiting judges from relying solely on the seriousness of charges.

Skaggs’ attorneys emphasized her clean criminal record, community ties, role as GOP treasurer, and ownership of “50 State DMV,” a Las Cruces title and registration business. They argued these factors demonstrated she was neither a flight risk nor a danger.

The appellate court disagreed. The alleged facts—high speed, immediate flight from the scene, license plate change, and hiding the vehicle—painted a picture of consciousness of guilt that prosecutors argued no conditions could remedy. Combined with her history of six speeding violations and a 2025 racing warning, the court concluded that even monitored release would be inadequate. The affirmation, issued without a full written opinion, reflects judicial skepticism of the defense arguments.

Beyond the Criminal Case: A Wrongful Death Suit Looms

While the criminal case proceeds, Skaggs faces a parallel legal battle. On June 30, just eight days after Brown’s death, the victim’s family filed a wrongful death lawsuit in New Mexico’s 1st Judicial District Court. The suit, filed on behalf of Brown’s minor child and the child’s mother, seeks damages for medical and funeral expenses, lost income, loss of Brown’s relationship with his family, punitive damages, and other costs.

This civil lawsuit operates under different legal standards than the criminal case. While prosecutors must prove guilt “beyond a reasonable doubt” in criminal court, civil plaintiffs need only prove their case by a “preponderance of the evidence”—a lower standard. The wrongful death suit may proceed even if Skaggs is ultimately acquitted in criminal court, and a civil judgment could result in significant financial liability regardless of the criminal outcome.

Broader Implications and What Comes Next

The appellate court’s decision to uphold detention is significant beyond this single case. In an era when criminal justice reform advocates have pushed for greater pretrial release opportunities, this case demonstrates that New Mexico courts still apply detention when specific facts—flight from the scene, evidence tampering, and pattern behavior—suggest heightened risk.

For Skaggs, her path to freedom before trial has been blocked at both district and appellate levels. Unless she pursues extraordinary legal remedies, she will remain in custody at the Doña Ana County Detention Center during months or years of litigation.

The case now moves into the pre-trial phase. Skaggs faces felony charges of leaving the scene of a crash resulting in death—up to three years—and tampering with evidence—up to 18 months. Prosecutors’ investigation leveraged eyewitness photos, Flock camera footage, and OnStar GPS tracking to build their case. Pre-trial motions, potential plea negotiations, and discovery disputes lie ahead before a trial likely to attract significant media attention.

A Community at the Crossroads

For the Las Cruces and Tularosa communities, this case has raised uncomfortable questions about accountability at all levels of society. That someone holding Skaggs’ position of trust in the Republican political establishment could be accused of leaving a man dead and covering up her involvement has shaken assumptions about justice.

For Andrew Brown’s family, the appellate decision provides assurance that courts are treating the case seriously. They pursue both criminal accountability and a wrongful death judgment. The case of Kimberly Skaggs now moves from appeals courts into substantive legal battles, where Andrew Brown’s death will continue to demand accountability and justice.

item.title: Recall case against Commissioner Burnett goes before a Judge Wednesday and Then Possibly to the Voters
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO — In New Mexico, a voter cannot simply circulate a recall petition against an elected official and take it straight to the ballot. State law places a judge in the path first.

Under the state Recall Act and NMSA Section 3-14-16, anyone seeking to recall a municipal officer must first persuade a district court that “sufficient facts and probable cause” exist for the recall to proceed. It is a screening step, and it is deliberately narrow. 

The judge does not decide whether the official broke the law, does not decide whether the official should keep the seat, and does not remove anyone from office. The judge decides one thing: whether there is enough to let the process go forward.

If the court finds probable cause, the petitioner may begin gathering signatures in the official’s district. If enough registered voters sign, a recall election is held, and the voters decide. If the petitioner cannot collect the signatures, or if the judge finds the threshold is not met, the effort ends and the official stays in office. 

The hearing exists so that no official can be forced into a recall on nothing at all — but the ultimate judgment, if the case clears the screen, belongs to the voters, not the court. At the hearing itself, both the petitioner and the official may present evidence and cross-examine witnesses.

The Burnett case

That threshold test is what brings Alamogordo City Commissioner Stephen W. Burnett before a district judge Wednesday morning. District Judge John P. Sugg is scheduled to hear the case, Murillo v. Burnett, No. D-1215-CV-2026-00626, at 9 a.m. Wednesday, July 29, at the Twelfth Judicial District courthouse in Alamogordo. The hearing is open to the public.

The petition was brought by Kim White Owl Murillo, a District 2 elector representing herself. Burnett, who is also appearing without a lawyer, has filed a written response asking the court to find no probable cause and deny the petition.

The two describe the same set of City records in sharply different terms — a divide that sits at the center of Wednesday’s hearing.

What the petitioner alleges

Murillo’s petition rests largely on the City’s handling of the recent city manager hiring, which she frames as a documented reversal of a public decision. According to her filings, the Commission voted 7-0 in open session on March 10 to enter a contract with then-Acting City Manager Dr. Stephanie Hernandez — the only candidate to pass the City’s scored interview process, which Murillo says rated Hernandez well above the passing threshold, while Robert Stockwell, later hired, was never scored at all.

Murillo alleges that no contract was ever offered to Hernandez. Instead, after a closed session on April 28, the Commission voted 4-3 to resolve the matter with a payment her filings put at roughly $485,000 gross, with Burnett in the majority and Commissioners Warren Robinson and Mark Tapley and Mayor Sharon McDonald voting no. She contends the nine-page contract drafted for Hernandez was then reused for Stockwell — pointing to a redlined draft in City files with Hernandez’s name struck through and Stockwell’s inserted, on terms she says were more favorable to him.

Central to her reply is a sequence she says Burnett’s response never addresses: that on June 12 Commissioner Baxter Pattillo emailed the full Commission the Stockwell contract, and that on June 16 he wrote again stating the version had already “gained the approval” of Stockwell and had been distributed to commissioners before the June 15 closed session. By the time that session — noticed for “City Manager recruitment and City Manager hiring” — was held, Murillo argues, a candidate-approved contract was already in every commissioner’s hands.

Murillo also points to a sworn statement from Commissioner Robinson, who was in the April 28 closed session and states under penalty of perjury that a four-member bloc had, in his account, decided the outcome before the session began and had no intention of offering Hernandez a contract. Robinson states he walked out; Burnett, one of the four, did not. A second sworn statement, from former Mayor Susan Payne, addresses the earlier 2025 search and states Stockwell was not part of the process the full Commission reviewed.

What the commissioner argues

Burnett’s response argues that the petition fails as a matter of law and fact. He contends that two of Murillo’s three grounds — misfeasance and malfeasance — require proof of an “improper or corrupt motive,” and that the petition offers only disagreement with a discretionary decision, which under New Mexico Supreme Court precedent cannot support a recall. He relies on CAPS v. Board Members and Arellano v. Lopez for that motive requirement.

On the open-meetings question, Burnett contends the operative decision to hire Stockwell was made in open session by public roll-call vote on June 15, after a closed session used to interview the candidate — a sequence he says the Attorney General’s compliance guidance permits. He argues the acts Murillo describes, including the recruitment of Stockwell, are attributable to other commissioners, not to him, quoting Pattillo’s public statement that the effort was “my solo legwork” and noting Mayor Pro-Tem Josh Rardin’s statement that he was the one who approached Stockwell in June of 2025.

Burnett leans heavily on Pena v. Rio Arriba County Commissioner, a 2025 New Mexico Supreme Court decision holding that an Open Meetings Act violation cannot be shown without a finding that a quorum — not a single member — made the challenged decision. He also cites the July 5 order in the related case, Edwards v. Alamogordo City Commission, in which the court declined to issue a temporary restraining order, that case is ongoing and contrary to Burnetts assertion no finding has been made as the next hearing is on August 12th in that case.

Where the arguments collide

Murillo’s reply argues that Burnett’s own record supplies the very quorum evidence Pena requires. She notes his response states that during a closed session “all seven members had reached a consensus to speak with Mr. Stockwell” — which she casts not as her characterization but as his own account of a collective, closed-door decision about a named candidate. Paired with the pre-meeting circulation of an approved contract, she argues, that is a quorum formulating public policy outside a meeting, not the lone-member conduct Pena found insufficient.

She also disputes Burnett’s use of the companion case. The July 5 order, she notes, decided only a request for emergency relief under a different legal standard, expressly says it does not resolve the merits, and was entered in a case to which she is not a party; the Commission’s motion to dismiss there remains undecided, with a hearing set for Aug. 12. And she argues Mayor McDonald’s testimony that she knew of no outside coordination proves only that McDonald — who voted no — was excluded from it, not that no coordination occurred among the members who voted yes.

Murillo further contends Burnett’s response was assembled before he had seen the Robinson and Payne statements — noting his own exhibit index says as much — and points out that Payne’s statement was filed on the public docket of the companion case on June 17, weeks before his response. Burnett will have the opportunity to respond at the hearing.

Where the two sides look at the same City records and describe what happened so differently, Murillo argues, that disagreement is itself what probable cause looks like. Burnett’s position is that the petition should not clear even that threshold, and that the matter amounts to a disagreement with lawful, discretionary votes. 

Which view prevails is for Judge Sugg to decide Wednesday but more importantly he should let the the voters of District 2 decide.

Editor’s note: Alamogordo Town News publisher Chris Edwards is the petitioner in Edwards v. Alamogordo City Commission, the related Open Meetings Act case referenced in both parties’ filings. He is not a party to the recall case. This report is drawn from the parties’ court filings and public City records.
