item.title: Timberon Water District’s Retaliation Campaign: Named in Fines, Attacked for Asking Questions
item.description:
District Names Individuals in Official Agenda, Then Removes Names; Anonymous Website Emerges Attacking Journalists; IPRA Requests Blocked from Multiple Requesters

TIMBERON, N.M. — On July 28, 2026, the Timberon Water and Sanitation District published an official meeting agenda that named two individuals—Aaron Foster and David Hunter—in connection with $62,620 in regulatory violations and fines. Hours later, TWSD removed their names from a revised version.

Both versions now exist in the public record.

Last week, an anonymously attributed social media page emerged attacking Chris Edwards, one of several journalist investigating TWSD's governance and finances, specifically invoking a white-collar felony conviction from over a decade ago—long resolved—as grounds for questioning his credibility.

Meanwhile, Edwards' Inspection of Public Records Act (IPRA) requests remain unfulfilled and out of compliance, and Mark Harding is reported to also be facing similar obstruction on his own records requests.

These actions—agenda naming followed by rapid removal, anonymous character assassination of journalists, and systematic blocking of records requests—paint a picture of a public agency attempting to intimidate critics and silence oversight.

Legal experts say the pattern violates New Mexico's IPRA retaliation statute, raises defamation concerns, and may constitute tortious interference with press freedom.

THE AGENDA INCIDENT: Official Naming, Then Erasure

On July 28, 2026, TWSD's official meeting notice read:

"Approve Resolution No. _______ (TBD) the NMED Administrative Compliance Order regarding the fines in the amount of $62,620 for violations occurring in 2023, 2024, 2025 and violations from Aaron Foster and David Hunter."

Critical Detail:

The agenda header states: Authorized by Otis Price, Chairman of the Board of Directors." The Board Chairman directly authorized naming these individuals.

Later Tuesday, TWSD issued a revised agenda removing both names entirely:

“Approve Resolution No. _______ (TBD) the NMED Administrative Compliance Order regarding the fines in the amount of $62,620 for violations occurring in 2023, 2024, and 2025."

Why the Naming and Removal Both Matter

Mark Harding stated: "I don't have anything to do with their $62k fine. Neither does David Hunter. He has a cease and desist filed against Mr Price."

Why This Is Damning:

The rapid removal signals TWSD knew the naming was improper or legally vulnerable. If the naming had a legitimate factual basis, why remove it? The removal demonstrates consciousness of guilt.

Moreover, Hunter has an active cease and desist against Otis Price, the Board Chairman who authorized the agenda. Price used his official authority to name someone with whom he has a personal legal conflict—then removed the names when the original became public.

This is textbook abuse of official authority.

WHO ARE FOSTER, HUNTER, AND HARDING?

David Hunter is a Timberton resident and community oversight advocate questioning TWSD's performance on water outages, infrastructure failures, and regulatory compliance.

Critically, Hunter has filed a cease and desist against Otis Price, the Board Chairman who authorized naming Hunter in the official agenda. This is not a generic resident complaint; it is active legal conflict between Price and Hunter. By naming Hunter in an official district document, Price weaponized his authority against his legal adversary.

Mark Harding has stated he and Hunter have nothing to do with the fines, and has identified Hunter's legal action against Price as relevant context.

Aaron Foster's background is less clear, but he too was named without factual basis or explanation.

Then came anonymous attacks via social media

Last week, days after the agenda incident, an anonymously run social media page emerged attacking Chris Edwards, the journalist investigating TWSD's governance.

The site highlights Edwards' white-collar felony conviction from over a decade ago—resolved long before his current journalism career—and argues that someone with such a history should not investigate public ethics. This frames Edwards' historical matter as disqualifying him from reporting on the present. Note other media has covered the issues with TWSD but no attacks on those journalist. 

The site's strategy is clear: delegitimize the messengers rather than address the reporting. It also attacks multiple Timberton residents and critics, all of whom have raised substantive concerns about TWSD's infrastructure, incomplete audits, or regulatory violations.

Notably absent from the site is any response to those substantive issues. It does not explain why audits remain incomplete, why water outages continue, why infrastructure leaks persist, or why Foster and Hunter were named in an official agenda without factual basis.

The site provides no author identification, no organization name, no accountability mechanism—anonymity designed to escape consequences for the attacks.

THE IPRA OBSTRUCTION: McCatee's Weeks of Refusal, Sudden Exit-Date Announcement

Chris Edwards' Request

On July 9, Chris Edwards filed an IPRA request seeking 10 categories of records related to the golf course lease, boil-water advisories, and infrastructure. The request was filed hours after his newspaper published investigative coverage of TWSD's finances and the $1-per-month golf course lease awarded without competitive bidding.

Leo McCatee's Hostile Response (July 13):

Leo McCatee, TWSD's records custodian, responded by calling the request a “scheme," telling Edwards: "I have other work to do than play street lawyer with you," and suggesting Edwards “should have been a responsible adult and filed smaller chunks."

He refused to provide any completion date.

This violates New Mexico IPRA, which does not require breaking requests into smaller chunks and intentionally allows broad requests to maximize disclosure.

Weeks of Refusal:

For weeks, Edwards asked for a timeline. McCatee refused providing no date, no schedule, nothing.

The Exit-Date Announcement:

A day before McCatee left TWSD employment, he suddenly announced July 23 as a completion date—the first and only date he ever provided.

This timing suggests a cover-your-tracks move designed to create a paper trail showing cooperation as he departed.

Courts have held that deliberate delays followed by rushed exit-date announcements constitute evidence of bad faith obstruction.

The Successor's Confusion:

After McCatee left, Wendy Case, TWSD's General Manager, contacted Edwards asking: “We have found 3 IPRAs. Would you please respond and let us know if this is correct?"

This is devastating. If McCatee had truly processed three separate requests, the successor should have known immediately. Instead, Case had to ask for clarification—suggesting McCatee either fabricated the "three requests" claim or deliberately obscured the documentation.

Either way, it violates IPRA's record-keeping requirements.

Most items requested have not been produced as of publication and nothing since McCatee has left. 

Mark Harding’s  Pending Requests

Harding also has his own IPRA requests with TWSD facing similar obstruction. Two requesters, same tactics, same public body.

THE PATTERN

Phase 1 - Record Blocking (July 9-28):

McCatee characterizes Edwards' legitimate request as a "scheme," refuses any timeline despite initial requests, then suddenly announces a completion date only as he's departing. Successor GM is confused about how many requests exist.

Phase 2 - Official Naming (July 28):

Same day as the office closure announcement to “complete IPRA request,” TWSD publishes agenda naming Foster and Hunter without factual basis or explanation. Hours later, removes the names from revised version.

Phase 3 - Anonymous Character Assassination (Last week):

Anonymous social media attacks Edwards for decade-old felony, attacks other critics, focuses entirely on discrediting messengers rather than addressing substance.

THE LEGAL EXPOSURE

1. IPRA Retaliation (NMSA 1978 § 14-2-12)

TWSD's conduct—hostile framing of a legitimate request as a "scheme," weeks of refusal to provide any timeline, office closure framed around "IPRA paperwork burden"—constitutes potential retaliation. The statute requires courts to award damages, costs, and reasonable attorney's fees.

2. Defamation (Agenda Naming)

By naming Foster and Hunter in an official public document without factual basis and without opportunity for them to respond, TWSD published statements that likely constitute defamation and libel.

3. Abuse of Official Authority

Price used his position as Board Chairman to retaliate against Hunter, with whom he has active legal conflict. This violates administrative law and may constitute conspiracy.

4. Tortious Interference

TWSD's actions—anonymous attack via social media, agenda naming, records blocking—are designed to interfere with Edwards' journalism business and his ability to conduct journalism.

5. First Amendment Violations

The pattern of slow balling records requests from journalists, naming associates in official documents, and potentially supporting anonymous character assassination raises serious constitutional concerns.

PRECEDENT

New Mexico courts have consistently rejected this defense:

Santa Fe (2024): City declared a request "excessively burdensome," then immediately claimed records didn't exist. The contradiction was damaging evidence.

Harding also has his own IPRA requests pending with TWSD—requests facing similar obstruction as Edwards'.

Las Cruces: Requester sued after city blocked and redacted records without statutory explanation. City paid penalties and released materials, acknowledging documents were "arguably overly redacted."

Albuquerque (2024):  Southwest Public Policy Institute sued alleging city unfairly used the "burdensome" exception to target certain requesters.

WHAT SHOULD HAPPEN NOW

New Mexico Attorney General:

- Investigate TWSD's IPRA handling for retaliation

- Subpoena communications to determine if anonymous website is connected to district staff

- Examine McCatee's obstruction conduct

- Review agenda incident for defamation and abuse of authority

- Consider conspiracy allegations given Price's direct authorization

TWSD Board:

- Demand accounting for why Foster and Hunter were named

- Explain why names were removed

- Commit to immediate compliance with all IPRA requests

Law Enforcement:

- Consider whether anonymous social media pages constitutes criminal harassment

The Community:

- File IPRA requests for: all prior requests, anonymous social media communications, agenda naming/removal decisions, audit status, infrastructure repair plans, golf course lease documentation

THE BOTTOM LINE

A public water utility that cannot defend its decisions on the merits—incomplete audits, ongoing outages, failed infrastructure—resorts to blocking records, naming critics in official documents, and supporting anonymous character assassination.

This is not how transparent agencies operate. This is how agencies respond when decisions cannot survive public scrutiny.

New Mexico law, court precedent, and democratic principles all suggest TWSD's conduct violates the law and undermines public trust.

The district can change course immediately: produce records, remove obstructions, address governance failures, allow critics and journalists to work unimpeded.

Whether TWSD chooses that path, or whether this ends in litigation, will tell the community everything they need to know about the district's commitment to transparency.

EDITOR'S NOTE

Chris Edwards is editor of 2nd Life Media Alamogordo Town News and the IPRA requester at the center of this story.

Mark Harding is a Timberton resident, community oversight advocate, and his own IPRA requester facing similar obstruction.

Primary sources:

- TWSD meeting agendas (original and revised) dated July 28, 2026

- IPRA request dated July 9, 2026, and all TWSD correspondence

- TWSD Facebook posts

- Wendy Case email clarifying IPRA requests

- Anonymous website materials (archived)

- Published article: "Timberon Water District Calls an Open Records Request a 'Scheme' — Then Won't Say When It'll Comply," 2nd Life Media Alamogordo Town News, July 13, 2026

- NMSA 1978 §§ 14-2-1 through 14-2-12 (IPRA)

- Court cases: *Britton v. Office of the Attorney General*, 2019-NMCA-002; *ACLU of New Mexico v. Duran*, 2016-NMCA-063; *Henry v. New Mexico Livestock Board*, No. A-1-CA-40127 (N.M. Ct. App. Mar. 6, 2024)

- New Mexico Department of Justice IPRA Compliance Guide

TWSD and district officials are invited to explain the basis for naming Foster and Hunter, account for removal, address obstruction allegations, respond to coordination questions regarding the anonymous website, provide completion timeline for IPRA requests, and address substantive governance issues.

item.title: Alamogordo City Commission Establishes Mayor’s Youth Advisory Commission, Honors EMT Graduates
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO — The Alamogordo City Commission held its regular meeting on Tuesday, July 28, celebrating community achievements while charting a path forward for youth engagement and civic leadership development.

The all-commission board convened at 6:30 p.m. with all seven members present, including Mayor Sharon McDonald, Mayor Pro Tem Josh Reardon, and Commissioners Baxter Battillo, Steven Burnett, Warren Robinson, Al Hernandez, and Mark Tapley. The evening featured three major agenda items that highlighted the city’s commitment to public safety, economic development, and youth empowerment.

Fire Department Honors EMT Basic Graduates

The commission began with a celebratory presentation recognizing five firefighters who recently completed their Emergency Medical Technician (EMT) Basic certification courses. The training, completed just one week prior to the meeting, represents a significant achievement for the fire department, which now has more than half its staff certified as EMT basics.

The course, taught by Eastern New Mexico University adjunct instructor Melissa Carter, required 180 hours of rigorous training spread over four months beginning in March. Graduates invested 90 hours in didactic instruction, 90 hours in skills development, and 48 hours in clinical ambulance experience—all undertaken while maintaining their regular firefighting shifts, some exceeding 48 hours per week.

“This class kept me on my toes,” Carter told the commission, noting that the cohort brought exceptional dedication to their studies. Remarkably, the class achieved a 100 percent pass rate on all exams, with no participant requiring retakes.

The graduates honored at the meeting included John Stroop, Nathan Preisner, Juan Valles, and Eric Martinez, who were present to receive their certificates and commemorative pins. John Stewart, a fifth graduate, was unable to attend due to personal reasons but will receive his certificate of completion.

Deputy Chief Lashley praised the graduates’ commitment, acknowledging the sacrifice required of both the participants and their families over the four-month period. “I know it’s been difficult, but you guys all pushed through and I couldn’t be prouder,” Lashley said.

Chamber of Commerce Outlines Ambitious Growth and Economic Development Strategy

Adam Hoppes, Executive Director of the Alamogordo Chamber of Commerce, delivered an extensive presentation to the commission on the organization’s achievements and forward-looking initiatives. Hoppes, who has served with the chamber for nearly three years, announced the hiring of two new staff members designed to strengthen the organization’s capacity for community engagement and business development.

Pearl, a recent hire with a communications degree from Boise State University, brings experience from Portland, Oregon. Damien, a local returning to Alamogordo with a marketing degree from New Mexico State University, will contribute local knowledge and media expertise to the chamber’s social media and marketing efforts.

Major Projects and Achievements

Hoppes highlighted the successful completion of the F-4 Phantom II fighter jet monument—a project that represents a defining achievement for the community. The aircraft, which served at Holloman Air Force Base and was stored at White Sands Regional Airport for nearly seven years before restoration, now stands as a community symbol.

“This project stands as a testament to what Alamogordo and Otero County can accomplish when we all come together with a common goal,” Hoppes told the commission. The initiative required over 200 volunteers contributing more than 15,000 man hours and generating $175,000 in private donations. When accounting for in-kind contributions from local businesses like KE&G, which donated over $100,000 worth of concrete work and labor, the total project value exceeds $1 million.

The chamber’s work on the monument contributed to Alamogordo winning the prestigious Altus Trophy for 2025—an honor recognizing the community that best supports Holloman Air Force Base. The award places Alamogordo among elite communities including San Antonio, Phoenix, and Wichita Falls, many with significantly larger populations and resources. Notably, the chamber won the award two of the last three years, requiring a comprehensive 108-page submission packet developed in just one month.

Housing Crisis and Development Solutions

Hoppes addressed the critical housing shortage facing the community, noting that Holloman Air Force Base has identified a need for over 900 housing units. While two major projects—the Patriot Point apartment complex and Sendero complex—are underway, the chamber director emphasized they represent only a partial solution.

Patriot Point has made adjustments to its plans pending state approval, with groundbreaking expected in August or September. Sendero is under active construction, with buildings rising rapidly. Both developments have benefited from the city and county’s metropolitan rehabilitation tax rebate program, which Hoppes credited as essential to making these projects financially feasible.

Beyond these major developments, Hoppes revealed ongoing discussions with an investor group from Montana and Utah who are pursuing the conversion of a hotel near Dutch Brothers into long-term residential accommodations. “Their idea is to take the hotel and convert it to long-term stays, specifically to cater to the families at Holloman Air Force Base,” Hoppes explained. The group plans to offer weekly, monthly, and six-month rental options at competitive rates.

Another developer has completed a duplex and plans to break ground on eight additional units, with another 12 units planned near the hospital. Both development groups have requested incentive programs similar to the metropolitan rehabilitation tax rebate, prompting early conversations with city administration about potentially scaling down incentives for smaller projects.

Microplex Initiative and Regional Economic Strategy

Among the chamber’s most ambitious initiatives is the “microplex” strategy—a regional branding and marketing approach designed to dramatically expand Alamogordo’s economic reach. While Alamogordo’s city population stands at approximately 32,000, Otero County has a population of 67,000. By partnering with neighboring Lincoln County, the combined “microplex” would reach a population of roughly 100,000.

This increased population base matters because large corporations typically target communities with 45,000 to 50,000 residents. By repositioning the region as a microplex, the chamber aims to attract major retailers and service businesses that have historically bypassed Alamogordo.

“Alamogordo has notoriously not had large corporations come in because of the fact that we’re sitting at that stagnant 32,000,” Hoppes explained. The strategy is not novel—Clovis and Portales successfully implemented a similar approach in 2005, resulting in dramatic and permanent community transformation.

Air Service Study and Regional Jet Service

The chamber is spearheading efforts to bring commercial jet service to the region through the development of an air service study. In coordination with Holloman Air Force Base and the Airport Advisory Board, the chamber is creating a scope of work to assess the feasibility of regional jet service—potentially operating from Holloman rather than the regional airport.

Colonel John Etheridge, former wing commander of Holloman Air Force Base, provided written support for the initiative, stating that “the establishment of this air service study is a top priority for installation in the local community.” The rationale is straightforward: military personnel currently flying through El Paso faces significant costs in transportation, overnight parking, and lodging.

When asked about the cost of the air service study, Hoppes indicated initial quotes ranged from $7,000 to $90,000 due to unclear scope of work, but historical precedent suggests costs in the $15,000 to $20,000 range, potentially reaching $30,000.

Tourism and Recreation Initiatives

The chamber announced new efforts to position Alamogordo as “the hub of enchantment,” leveraging the region’s proximity to White Sands National Park, the New Mexico Museum of Space History, Cloudcroft, and Ruidoso. Targeted advertising in Las Cruces, El Paso, and surrounding communities aims to capture tourist traffic and spending.

A particularly innovative initiative involves White Sands recreational equipment rental. Drawing inspiration from ski towns like Ruidoso, the chamber is developing a rental program offering snowboards, sleds, tubes, and handicap-accessible wheelchairs specifically designed for sand dunes. The program would create an incentive loop: tourists rent equipment, enjoy White Sands, then receive discounts to patronize Alamogordo businesses.

Member Services and Support

The chamber now supports over 450 members through an expanded array of services. These include an online concierge using real staff members rather than AI chatbots to answer visitor questions, directed through the chamber website to member businesses. The chamber is launching a “black card” and loyalty program allowing members to offer reciprocal discounts, with analysis suggesting 400 participating members could immediately justify chamber membership dues.

Business spotlight initiatives on social media twice weekly are being expanded to city billboards, with a verbal commitment secured for display on the billboard outside the Alamogordo Zoo on White Sands Boulevard.

Leadership Development and Future Planning

The chamber is recruiting for Leadership Otero, a nine-month program for up to 20 participants designed to identify and develop the next generation of community leaders. “It’s important that we have a succession plan so there’s somebody left to carry the torch,” Hoff noted.

The chamber is also exploring the feasibility of Union Pacific train service to Alamogordo and early-stage conversations with a Las Cruces developer interested in building a new hotel with associated car wash and restaurant facilities on the site of the former burnt-down hotel near Applebee’s.

Subdivision Regulations Updated to Support Development

Prior to consideration of the youth commission, the city commission unanimously approved Ordinance 17-24, which repeals the city’s outdated subdivision requirements in Chapter 22 and replaces them with updated regulations in Chapter 20 of the Land Development Code.

Shelly Barron of the Community Development Department presented the ordinance, addressing concerns raised by commissioners in previous meetings. Commissioner Tapley had specifically questioned provisions related to extraterritorial jurisdiction and estimated construction costs. Those provisions have been removed from the ordinance and will be incorporated into a separate section of the land development code in the future.

Commissioners also sought clarity on a proposed 3% fee on developers to fund long-term maintenance of drainage retention and detention ponds. Barron provided specific examples: the Fairgrounds commercial subdivision development at Fairgrounds and White Sands Boulevard would incur approximately $20,000 under the 3% assessment, which aligns with annual maintenance costs for detention facilities. Somerset Village, a 47-home subdivision off Hamilton Road, would be assessed roughly $47,000—enough to cover approximately one and a half to two years of maintenance.

“I don’t think it’s an onerous amount on the developers to levy that,” Barron told the commission, arguing the fees represent reasonable cost-sharing for ongoing maintenance responsibilities.

The ordinance passed unanimously 7-0.

Public Expresses Support for Youth Commission, Raises Property Rights Concerns

Before the commission voted on the youth advisory commission resolution, the public comment period included passionate testimonials and a request for new property ordinances.

Youth Advocate Endorses New Commission

Nolani Nagamini, a young Alamogordo resident, addressed the commission with enthusiasm about the proposed Mayor’s Youth Advisory Commission.

“As a young person growing up in Alamogordo, it means so much to me that our ideas, opinions and voices matter,” Nagamini told commissioners. “The Commission gives students like me the opportunity to learn, serve and help make our community better.”

Nagamini announced plans to be among the first applicants, stating: “I want to learn how our city works, develop leadership skills, and work alongside other students who care about making Alamogordo the best it could be. I believe this program will inspire young people to stand up, volunteer, and become future leaders.”

She emphasized that the program demonstrates youth can make meaningful contributions immediately rather than waiting until adulthood. “It shows students that we aren’t just the future of Alamogordo. We can make a difference today.”

Palm Tree Maintenance Ordinance Requested

Gina Donahue brought a focused but urgent issue before the commission: the need for a palm tree maintenance and property protection ordinance. Donahue presented photographs and documented evidence of damage caused by neglected palm trees in her neighborhood.

“Palm trees certainly add beauty and character to our community and this proposal is not intended to discourage residents from planting and enjoying them,” Donahue stated. “It’s about encouraging responsible maintenance so that one property owner’s neglected trees do not create hazardous and financial burdens for neighboring property owners.”

Donahue described specific hardships her family has endured. On June 28th, her air conditioning unit shut down twice—the only one in the neighborhood experiencing failure—due to debris from nearby palm trees. The debris, including large heavy fronds, seed pods, bark fibers, and flowers, collects around outdoor air conditioning condenser units, restricting airflow, reducing efficiency, and causing equipment shutdowns.

“In a community where summer temperatures regularly exceed 100 degrees, a properly functioning air condition is not a luxury. It’s an issue for our health and our safety,” Donahue emphasized. She noted that modern air conditioning unit replacement costs can reach $20,000, and the debris creates wear that contributes to premature replacement.

Beyond air conditioning issues, Donahue raised concerns about safety hazards. Dead fronds weighing dozens of pounds can fall without warning, creating risks of damage to roofs, fences, vehicles, and neighboring properties. She also noted that fallen debris creates slip-and-fall hazards for elderly residents.

“Many neighboring property owners spend countless hours cleaning debris that do not generate on their own property,” Donahue said. “They bear the cost of cleaning gutters, maintaining landscaping, repairing damage property and protecting equipment that should not be affected by a neighboring tree.”

Donahue provided a draft ordinance proposal to the city clerk for consideration by city administration and legal counsel. The request reflects a broader tension between property rights and neighborly obligations in residential communities.

Community Celebrates Cleanup and Youth Opportunity

Kim Great White Owl Murillo spoke to celebrate the success of the city’s recent cleanup initiative and express support for the youth commission.

Murillo described the positive impact of the mayor’s citywide cleanup, emphasizing acts of service and neighborly love. “I met neighbors who had fallen on hard times and couldn’t keep their yards up and were so grateful and yet reluctant to accept our help but in the end they were so grateful,” Murillo recounted. “That’s just overwhelming for me—the gratitude and just to be of service to my community.”

She praised the physical results, noting her team was among the first to complete their dumping, and highlighted the enthusiasm and community spirit demonstrated throughout the cleanup day.

Regarding the Youth Advisory Commission, Murillo expressed deep approval. “It’s a vision that’s been in play and should have happened a long time ago,” she said. “I’m just so proud of what we are going to provide for the youth—meaning and purpose in their life. And they’re going to contribute to this city to leave a foundation for the next generations to come.”

Murillo also offered personal praise for Mayor Sharon McDonald’s leadership, acknowledging the challenges she has navigated. “And with all the nuances that you’ve had to battle with this last six, seven months and to stand alone as a woman against this force—you’re showing women everywhere of what it is for a woman to rise up, to be a true service to their city, to their citizens, and to the future.”

New Mayor’s Youth Advisory Commission Approved

In a landmark decision, the commission unanimously approved Resolution 26-27, establishing the Mayor’s Youth Advisory Commission (MYAC). The initiative, presented by city administration and supported by Mayor Sharon McDonald and community liaison Cherie, aims to create a structured pathway for young people to engage in civic leadership and community problem-solving.

The commission will consist of 16 youth members representing grades 8 through 12, with representation drawn from each high school grade (three students from grades 9-12), one student from each middle school (eighth grade), and one NMSU freshman. The diverse composition intentionally extends beyond traditional high achievers to include youth from all backgrounds and experiences.

“We want the high achievers. We want the kids who sit by themselves in the cafeteria at lunch. We want them all to apply,” said one of the program coordinators during the presentation.

Program Structure and Objectives

The MYAC will hold monthly meetings lasting approximately 70 minutes after school hours. Youth members will receive mentoring and guidance from community volunteers and city administrators, including Eric Lucero from Christ Community Church and members of the Rotary Club who have already volunteered to serve as mentors.

The commission outlined several ambitious objectives for the initiative:

Leadership Development: The program will teach youth how to conduct effective meetings, establish agendas, and develop civic projects. Members will participate in workshops led by Toastmasters and NMSU personnel on public speaking and community problem-solving.

Educational Focus: Unlike many young people who learn about federal and state government in schools, the MYAC fills a critical gap by exposing students to the mechanics of local government—the forum where youth can potentially have the most tangible impact.

Volunteer Opportunities: Participants will earn documented volunteer hours applicable to college applications while contributing to real community improvement projects.

Community Engagement: The youth will conduct forums and surveys among their peers to identify community concerns and opportunities for improvement from a youth perspective. Some participants may also engage with Holloman Air Force Base leadership for inspiration and mentoring.

Program Timeline and Implementation

The commission approved an aggressive implementation timeline:

• Friday (following the meeting): Recruitment begins at the Back to School Block Party with information tables and applications

• August-September: School outreach and additional recruitment efforts

• September 8: First commission meeting with youth swearing-in ceremony

• September 14: Inaugural MYAC meeting with orientation

• October 13: Officer elections

• Ongoing: Regular meetings on the second Monday of each month through year-end

The Sacramento Mountains Foundation has already provided initial funding to launch the program. The city administration hopes the commission will leverage members’ community connections to recruit additional mentors and secure support from businesses and organizations.

Historical Context

The proposal to establish the MYAC reflects a return to a program that operated successfully in previous years. Commissioner Baxter Battillo was specifically called out during the presentation as a “poster child” for the program’s success, having served on a similar youth commission in his own youth before going on to city leadership.

City Hall Now Offers Extended Hours

City Manager Stockwell reported that City Hall has expanded its hours of operation, now open from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. Monday through Friday. The extended schedule is designed to provide citizens with sufficient time to conduct city business without rushing. Stockwell noted the city is receiving positive feedback from residents appreciating the additional access.

Commission Remarks Address Community Engagement and Public Services

During the remarks and inquiries portion of the meeting, commissioners celebrated community contributions and discussed administrative improvements.

Mayor McDonald addressed a citizen concern raised during public comment, noting she had spoken with City Manager Stockwell about implementing a budget billing plan for water bills—similar to programs offered by the power company. The plan would provide fixed-income residents with more manageable, predictable monthly expenses. “We are looking into that,” the mayor confirmed.

Commissioner Robinson provided an update on the city’s recent cleanup initiative, reporting that the effort addressed approximately 34 properties directly, with an additional estimated 26 properties benefiting from participation at multiple dumpster locations. Commissioner Robinson credited the commissioners who volunteered to staff various cleanup locations and praised all citizens who participated.

“When you have people that want to be there and they do their job and they’re out in the heat,” Robinson noted, acknowledging both the physical effort required and favorable weather conditions on July 18th when temperatures started at 66 degrees with a high of only 84 degrees.

The successful day was made possible by community sponsors including the Sacramento Mountains Foundation and Amy Tilson at State Farm Insurance. Robinson particularly highlighted the contribution of the Labor Hub, which provided 12 weed eaters and loaned additional equipment including lawnmowers, addressing chronic equipment shortages that typically challenge the annual cleanup.

Commissioner Robinson also acknowledged community organizations’ contributions, noting Porky’s Heating and Cooling’s annual golf tournament benefiting Base Otero raised over $25,000, and highlighting Thrive’s Bart Crow concert, which drew strong attendance and raised additional funds.

Meeting Actions

All agenda items passed unanimously by a 7-0 vote, including:

• Approval of the consent agenda

• Adoption of Ordinance 17-24 updating subdivision regulations

• Establishment of the Mayor’s Youth Advisory Commission via Resolution 26-27

The meeting adjourned following the approvals, reflecting strong commission consensus on the city’s strategic priorities and community initiatives. The unanimous votes signal unified direction among commissioners on major policy initiatives, from regulatory updates to new youth development programs.

The Alamogordo City Commission’s focus on professional development for city employees, economic vitality, and youth engagement signals the city’s commitment to both immediate operational excellence and long-term community sustainability.

item.title: In Memory of Michael “Mike” Ray Walker
item.description:
Michael “Mike” Ray Walker, beloved husband, father, grandfather, brother, uncle, tio, cousin, and friend, was born on June 23, 1953, in Lubbock, Texas, to Lawrence Luther Walker and Eureka Lucille Walker. After fighting a valiant and courageous battle with esophageal cancer, Mike was lovingly healed in the arms of his Savior, Jesus Christ, on July 20, 2026.

Mike is survived by his devoted wife and best friend, Sylvia Telles Walker. Married for 51 beautiful years, Mike often said that marrying Sylvia was the best decision he ever made. Their love was steadfast, joyful, and the foundation of the family they built together.

He is survived by his children, each of whom he loved fiercely: Julie and husband Brian Grinder of Alamogordo, NM; Laura and husband Diego Ortega of Las Cruces, NM; Michael Walker Jr. and husband Garrett Hall of Honolulu, HI.

Mike was the proud grandfather of six grandchildren who were the light of his life: Promise and husband Nic Bood, Baylyn Grinder, Ethan Grinder, Emily Grinder, D’Angelo Ortega, and Sebastian Ortega. He is also survived by his sister, Syldina Walker Butler, along with numerous godchildren, nieces, nephews, extended family, and dear friends who cherished him.

He was preceded in death by his grandparents, Luther and Ola Mae Walker, and Oscar and Eureka Smith; parents, Lawrence and Dorothy Walker, and Eureka Lucille and Victor Gibson; his sister, Marie Walker Trusty; his brothers, Lonnie and wife Christine Walker, and Richard Walker.

Mike was a proud graduate of New Mexico State University, earning his bachelor’s degree in electrical engineering technology. He worked tirelessly to put himself through college, spending years on offshore oil rigs before becoming a field engineer in the Texas oil patch. In 1986, Mike and Sylvia moved “home” to Alamogordo to be closer to family, a decision that enriched the lives of everyone around them.

A man of deep patriotism, Mike dedicated over three decades as a contractor for the Department of Defense. His work ethic was unmatched, and his loyalty to his country unwavering.

If you knew Mike, you knew his servant’s heart. He was always ready to lend a helping hand, volunteer his time, or share his wisdom. His dry “dad humor” and endless supply of jokes brought laughter to countless memories. His warm smile, humble spirit, and gentle patience made him someone people naturally gravitated toward.

Mike was a “Super Fan,” cheering on all of his children and his grandchildren throughout their school years. Nothing brought him more joy than sitting in the stands, supporting the kids he loved so dearly. His presence, steady, encouraging, and full of pride, will be deeply missed.

His strength, courage, and unwavering faith in Jesus Christ guided him throughout his life and especially through his battle with cancer. His love for the Lord was evident in the way he lived, served, and loved others.

The family extends their heartfelt gratitude to Christus Cancer Center, Christus Southern New Mexico, and Alamogordo Home Health Care and Hospice for their compassionate care, encouragement, and support throughout Mike’s journey.

The family has entrusted Mike’s care to Alamogordo Funeral Home, with deep appreciation for their kindness and professionalism. In lieu of flowers, donations may be made to the Wounded Warrior Project or your local Cancer Resource Center, causes close to Mike’s heart.

A Celebration of Life will be held on Friday, August 7, 2026, at St. Jude Catholic Church, with a rosary at 10:15 am, Mass at 11:00 am, and a reception to follow in the parish hall.

Mike Walker leaves behind a legacy of love, faith, strength, and service. His impact on his family, his community, and all who knew him will continue to shine brightly for generations.

item.title: Tularosa Village Board Reverses Cell Tower Approval Over Notice Failures; Adopts Budget, Road Grants, Police Promotion
item.description:
TULAROSA, N.M. — The Tularosa Village Board of Trustees voted unanimously to reverse its prior approval of a 199-foot wireless communications tower after more than a dozen residents told the board they were never notified the project was under consideration, capping a meeting that also included routine budget adoptions, two New Mexico Department of Transportation road-funding agreements, a police promotion, a park dedication honoring a fallen Marine, and department head reports on a groundwater treatment project years in the making.

The meeting opened with the pledge of allegiance and a roll call of Trustees Bruce Willis, Garwood, Rupp and Otero before moving into public comment, where the proposed cell tower dominated discussion for nearly the entire evening.

The board took up a request to reconsider Special Use Permit Application 2026-SUP-001, which the board had approved 3-2 at its May 21 meeting to allow applicant Sean Milks, working on behalf of property owner Nancy Carr, to build a 199-foot self-supporting wireless tower intended to serve carriers T-Mobile and Verizon Wireless, with AT&T expressing interest.

Village Attorney Nan Winter told the board the application had originally listed the site as 1008 Old Mescalero Rd. when it went before the Planning and Zoning Commission in March, but the address was later changed to 44 Sunset Rd. Milks told the board the change reflected the assignment of a new address to what had been an unaddressed parcel once zoning was sought, not a change in the physical location.

More than ten residents spoke against the tower during public comment, raising concerns about radio-frequency health effects, property values, structural failure and fire risk, and the lack of a village wireless communications ordinance. Speakers included Stephanie Dubois, Terry Hollis, John Gonzalez, David Gonzalez, Eva Gonzalez, Albert Eiles, Billy Hopson, Dale Nelson, Brian Hobson and Cynthia Prelow, along with resident Joan Price, who questioned whether the tower would support future data center development. Milks said the tower's function is unrelated to data center infrastructure.

Winter advised the board that federal law — 47 U.S.C. § 332(c)(7)(B) — bars local governments from denying or reversing wireless facility approvals based on radio-frequency emissions health concerns where FCC exposure limits are met, and that no expert testimony on RF health effects or property value impacts had been entered into the record at either the Planning and Zoning Commission hearing or the board's May 21 meeting. She said public comment alone does not constitute evidence for purposes of a reversal.

David Gonzalez, who filed the request for reconsideration, argued that Milks' own presentation showed the tower would not meet setback requirements on all four sides of the property — falling 191 feet from the property line on the Sunset Road side, short of the roughly 199-foot standard Milks said the design otherwise achieved. Milks said the tower is engineered to collapse onto itself rather than fall like a tree in the event of failure, but acknowledged under questioning that the foundation dimensions have not yet been finalized pending a soils report.

Several residents, including Eva Gonzalez, Brian Hobson and Cynthia Prelow, told the board they had received no advance notice of the project beyond a legal notice published twice in the Alamogordo Daily News and door-to-door outreach by Planning and Zoning that several residents said never reached them. Village Clerk Rebecca Garcia confirmed the notice method used.

After hearing from the public, trustees stated they were basing their decision to reverse the approval on inadequate notice to affected property owners, along with the absence of a completed wireless ordinance — not on the radio-frequency or property-value arguments Winter said were legally off-limits. The motion to grant reconsideration, effectively reversing the May 21 approval, passed by unanimous voice vote. Winter told the board either party — the applicant or the residents who sought reconsideration — retains the right to appeal the outcome to district court.

The board adopted three finance resolutions presented by Finance Officer Valerie Delgado: the fourth-quarter financial report for the fiscal year ended June 30, 2026 (Resolution 2026-207-1); a budget cleanup resolution for fiscal year 2025-26 (Resolution 2026-2027-2); and the final operating budget for fiscal year 2026-27 (Resolution 2026-2027-3). All three passed on roll-call votes. Trustees asked Delgado to follow up on a discrepancy in youth program registration fees and on the basis for increased ambulance service charges reflected in the budget.

The board adopted two cooperative agreements with the New Mexico Department of Transportation under the Local Government Road Fund program for fiscal year 2027:

Resolution 2026-2027-4 covers Old Mescalero Road from U.S. 54 to U.S. 70, with a total project cost of $300,000 — $225,000 from the state and $75,000 from the village. Trustees discussed whether to delay the project given the possibility of future sewer work in the same corridor, but approved it after village staff said declining the award could jeopardize future funding eligibility and that the village's wastewater treatment plant could not currently support additional sewer connections in that area regardless.

Resolution 2026-2027-5 covers pavement rehabilitation on Marin Drive, with a total project cost of $235,445 — approximately $176,584 from the state and $58,861 from the village. Trustees noted the road's poor condition poses a safety hazard, citing exposed barrels beneath a collapsed section of sewer line.

Both resolutions passed on roll-call votes. Village Clerk Rebecca Garcia said the village applied for both awards in February.

The board approved the appointment of Jesus Torres as Custodian 2 at $16 per hour, based on a recommendation from Head Custodian Ralph Otero.

The board also approved the promotion of Officer Latham Garnsey to sergeant at $27 per hour, based on a lengthy recommendation from Police Chief Geraldine Martinez, who cited Garnsey's work ethic, communication skills and completion of a first-line supervisor course, while acknowledging he has less tenure than is typical for the role. One trustee raised concerns about approving the pay change ahead of previously discussed raises for water treatment plant employees that have not yet been addressed, and about Garnsey supervising a relative within the department; Martinez said she treats him the same as any other officer in disciplinary matters. The promotion passed on a voice vote, with dissent noted from at least one trustee before the motion carried.

Trustee Mark Garwood proposed dedicating a section of the Community Center Park as Stephen Orosco Park, honoring a Tularosa native killed in Vietnam after, according to Garwood, throwing himself on an explosive device to protect fellow Marines. Garwood said a memorial placard would also recognize other Tularosa residents who died in combat across multiple wars, including residents Cordova, Bookout and Carr, and that he would personally fund and perform the masonry work outside the village budget. The board approved the proposal on a voice vote.

The board approved a $1,000 annual membership contribution to the Council of Governments (Resolution 2026-2027-6) and authorized use of Veterans Park on July 25, 2026, for the Tularosa Basin Downwinders Consortium's annual candlelight vigil honoring victims commemorated through the group's naming ceremony. A request to pave Otero Lane was tabled pending further review of using recycled asphalt millings the village has obtained from the state.

Engineering consultant Matt Thompson of Bohannon Huston presented an update on a long-planned alternate water supply project drawing on the village's Montezuma Well groundwater rights. The project would treat brackish groundwater — with total dissolved solids around 2,500 milligrams per liter — through a reverse osmosis system housed in a roughly 60-by-100-foot building near the village's existing water tank site, recovering about 82 percent of pumped water as usable supply.

Thompson said the remaining concentrated reject water would require disposal in lined evaporation ponds, and that the village has identified an approximately 80-acre tract to the south of the village for that purpose, with roughly 30 acres needed for the ponds and berms. He told the board the project has reached a design milestone requiring a decision on whether to proceed with the land purchase, and recommended additional public notification before finalizing it. Trustees clarified that they have approved funding for the project but have not yet approved the land acquisition itself, and directed staff to expand public outreach before further action. Construction, if the project proceeds on schedule, is estimated to begin around spring 2027 and take approximately 15 months.

Village Clerk Rebecca Garcia reported ongoing renovations at Village Hall, including new flooring, and said two new office staff have been hired.

Grant Coordinator Kendra Otero reported that paperwork for two capital projects — a splash pad (approximately $700,000 total, including village hall renovation costs) and separate Village Hall electrical, roofing and HVAC upgrades — was completed and submitted to the state ahead of a same-day deadline. She said the village is pursuing additional grants, including a $100,000 New Mexico True Destination Forward grant application for the museum building, and cautioned that the village's standing with the state Department of Finance and Administration currently limits its competitiveness for larger federal infrastructure grants.

Water operator Brett reported ongoing turbidity issues tied to recent rainfall but said the water system is otherwise operating normally, and that he is preparing for state certification testing.

Public works foreman Angel reported planned sewer plant lift station upgrades in August or September, ongoing odor-control measures at the treatment ponds, and use of state-supplied asphalt millings to improve village dirt roads including Lizard Lounge Road and Otero Lane.

Police Chief Geraldine Martinez reported the department is at five officers, with one additional certified hire pending, and that new patrol vehicles are near deployment ahead of the Aug. 5 start of school, when a school resource officer program is set to begin under a draft memorandum of understanding with Tularosa Municipal Schools.

Tularosa Senior Center Director Clarissa reported the center served 539 congregate meals last quarter, delivered meals to an average of 50 homebound seniors daily, and secured new funding including $75,000 from Otero County, $15,000 through the New Mexico Grown program, and $9,800 from the El Paso Community Foundation.

A Planning and Zoning Commission representative told the board the commission has reviewed several draft ordinances and permit forms — including a short-term rental ordinance, a development impact fee ordinance and a vacant building maintenance ordinance — prepared with the assistance of contractor Brandon Williams, and that the commission has not yet been formally asked to draft a wireless communications ordinance, though it could take on the task. Trustees and the commission representative acknowledged a communication gap over whether draft ordinances had been forwarded to the village attorney's office, which the representative attributed to email delivery issues.

This account is based on the audio record and viewing of the July 2026 Tularosa Village Board of Trustees regular meeting. Some speaker attributions among trustees could not be independently confirmed due to the time contrants of notes taken and are described generically as "the board" or "trustees" where individual identification was not clear.

item.title: Judge Hears Full Day of Testimony in Burnett Recall Case; Ruling Expected Friday
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO, N.M. — A district court judge spent more than six hours Wednesday hearing testimony and argument over whether a recall effort against City Commissioner Stephen Burnett may move forward, with a written ruling expected by the end of the day Friday.

The probable-cause hearing in Murillo v. Burnett (No. D-1215-CV-2026-00626), before Judge John P. Sugg, opened at 9 a.m. and ran until approximately 3:30 p.m. Petitioner Kim Murillo, who is representing herself without an attorney, is seeking court authorization to begin gathering signatures for a recall of Burnett under state recall law.

Judge Sugg made clear during the hearing that the court is not being asked to determine whether Burnett is guilty of wrongdoing. Instead, the question before him is narrower: whether Murillo has shown enough to allow a recall petition to proceed to voters. Under a statutory deadline, Sugg has 14 days from the initiation of the case to rule, putting the deadline at the end of this week. Once issued, the written order may be appealed to the New Mexico Supreme Court within five days.

The most notable moment of the day came during Burnett's closing remarks, when he told the court he has no legal obligation to talk with his constituents or to respond to their requests for information or dialogue. As a matter of law, Burnett's position is largely accurate: constituents have the ability to email or call an elected official, but no statute requires that official to respond. Burnett indicated his intention is not to be "consumed" by responding to constituents.

Supporters of Burnett say that position clears the legal bar. Critics argue it misses a different one — the ethical expectation that an elected official actually engage with the people who elected him.

That distinction became a undercurrent of the hearing: whether an official who declines to enter into dialogue with constituents is fulfilling the role he was elected to perform, and whether a pattern of refusing to communicate rises to the level of malfeasance. The court's ruling is not expected to resolve that debate directly, since it bears on the recall's merits rather than the threshold question of whether the petition can proceed — but it was raised repeatedly by both sides.

A significant portion of the day was devoted to Burnett's role in the city manager selection process, including the commission's handling of Dr. Stephanie Hernandez's candidacy and the eventual hiring of Robert Stockwell. Witnesses and questioning returned repeatedly to why the commission voted 7-0 at one point to move toward offering Hernandez a contract, only for that process to stall and ultimately end with Stockwell's selection instead.

Former Mayor Susan Payne, Commissioner Warren Robinson and former acting City Manager Dr. Stephanie Hernandez were each called unexpectedly to testify. None appeared to welcome being placed on the stand, and each visibly struggled at points with Murillo's questions — but all three answered honestly and directly.

Payne, under questioning, gave background on the timeline and testified that the selection process was still ongoing when it stalled. She acknowledged that a city attorney had determined the process had been legally deficient, and that the original process was described as "tainted" and requiring a do-over. No witness, including Burnett, offered a clear explanation for why Hernandez was not ultimately hired after the commission's 7-0 vote.

Burnett, for his part, sought to characterize the eventual selection of Stockwell as having been driven by former City Manager Rardin and Pattillo rather than by the commission itself but the whole commission votes in public. He also argued he had no issue with Hernandez as a candidate. But scoring sheets from a portion of the interview process, introduced during the hearing, told a different story: Burnett and Rardin gave Hernandez the lowest marks of any panelists, even though her overall score remained the highest of all candidates and he had voted 7 to 0 to offer her a contract but then reversed it to via a 4 to 3 vote without explanation even to the court.

The hearing was not without friction. Burnett appeared to receive coaching from the gallery on multiple occasions, including from his wife and a supporter in attendance, and at times seemed flustered and unprepared to answer questions on his own. Murillo, representing herself, struggled at points with courtroom procedure and appeared overwhelmed by the formality of the process, but pressed her case with visible conviction — arguing, in essence, that she simply wants her elected official to explain his positions and speak with the voters he represents, something she says Burnett has declined to do throughout the city manager selection process.

Judge Sugg took the matter under advisement and did not rule from the bench. A written order is expected by the end of the day Friday under the statute's 14-day deadline. If Sugg authorizes the recall to proceed, Murillo would then be cleared to begin gathering the signatures required to place the question before Alamogordo voters. Either side may appeal the ruling to the New Mexico Supreme Court within five days of its issuance.

Alamogordo Town News will continue to follow the case. Stay tuned.

EDITOR'S DISCLOSURE: Chris Edwards, publisher of Alamogordo Town News, has provided  input to petitioner Kim Murillo in this matter but is not a party to the case. Edwards is separately a plaintiff in a related but distinct civil action, Edwards v. Alamogordo City Commission (No. D-1215-CV-2026-00514), which remains pending before a different judge on the City's motion to dismiss.

item.title: Garcia Richard Wins DPNM SCC Special Selection, Joins Haaland on Democratic Ticket for Lieutenant Governor
item.description:
SANTA FE, N.M. — State Land Commissioner Stephanie Garcia Richard won a special election held Thursday by the Democratic Party of New Mexico's State Central Committee, securing the party's nomination for lieutenant governor and joining Deb Haaland atop the Democratic ticket ahead of the November general election.

Garcia Richard replaces Maggie Toulouse Oliver on the ballot. The committee's selection followed a competitive race against state Sen. Harold Pope, whom Garcia Richard thanked afterward for what she called a spirited campaign and for his ongoing service to New Mexicans.

Garcia Richard, a former public school teacher, served in the New Mexico House of Representatives before her election as Commissioner of Public Lands, a role she has held for two terms. In the House, she worked on legislation that helped establish the state's universal childcare program. As land commissioner, her office reports generating more than $15 billion in state funding for public education, along with job growth tied to clean energy development and a series of environmental protections for the state's air, land and water.

"I am deeply humbled and honored to earn the trust of the DPNM State Central Committee and to join Deb Haaland on this ticket," Garcia Richard said in a statement. "New Mexicans work incredibly hard, and they deserve a government that works just as hard for them. From my time in the classroom to the State House and the State Land Office, I have never stopped fighting for our communities. Deb and I share a vision for a New Mexico where we lower costs, increase access to healthcare, build safer communities, and provide a world-class public education for every child."

With the ticket now finalized, the Haaland-Garcia Richard campaign is turning its attention to the general election. Garcia Richard framed the contest as a choice between competing visions for the state's direction.

"The stakes this November could not be higher," Garcia Richard said. "While our Republican opponents want to drag our state backward with extreme, out-of-touch policies that will hurt working families and drive up costs, Deb Haaland and I are looking toward a brighter future. Our message is clear: we are helping kids read earlier and bringing trades back to schools in a big way, creating more affordable and accessible healthcare, getting illegal drugs off our streets, and making life more affordable with tax breaks to working people, universal childcare, and cheaper housing costs. We are ready to take our message to every corner of New Mexico and build a winning coalition that will deliver on our promises to the people."

Locally in Otero County the local Democratic Party via acting chair Joy Bordenave said, " we are thrilled the selection process is now completed and we can move forward with getting both Deb and Stephanie elected via this historic ticket. Locally, we will be working hard to get out the vote for these candidates as well as those Democats and Independents up and down the ballot." 

The Haaland-Garcia Richard ticket will face its Republican opponents Gregg Hull (for governor) and David Gallegos (for lieutenant governor) on the November ballot.
